$comment: THE FORMULA EVAL CORPUS — the hand-written half.,,Each task states a request a person would make, a fixture as typed cell,text, the formula that answers it, and the answer Calcula's own engine,produces. A `distractor` names the plausible wrong formula a model,reaches for and MUST NOT satisfy the expectation; a task whose,distractor also passes measures nothing and is a defect.,,Every reference and every distractor in this file has been run through,the engine via `core/calcula-format/examples/eval-formulas.rs`.,Formulas are INVARIANT: comma separators, dot decimals. 2026-09-15: twelve tasks carried a dead `intentSv` field and were mislabelled lang:"sv" although their `intent` — the only field the runner prompts with — was always English. The field is gone and the labels corrected (owner decision: the AI programme is English only). No task was removed: the corpus stays at 60 hand tasks, 97 with the library split. 2026-09-15: GROWN AND BALANCED, 60 -> 144 hand tasks, twelve per family (the runner adds 37 held-out lib:* tasks, so the measured corpus is 181). Every family held exactly FIVE tasks before, and McNemar needs six clean flips at any corpus size — which applies to every subset — so not one of the twelve families could ever reach p<0.05 on its own. The corpus could say 'this model is better overall' and could never say 'better at what', which is exactly what a bake-off between two complementary candidates needs.

tasks.intent: In the sales table in A1:C10, add up the Amount for every row where the Region is North AND the Rep is Alice. Rows that match only one of the two conditions must be excluded. Put the total in E2.

distractor.why: The single-condition SUMIF applies only the Region test and ignores the Rep entirely, so it also adds the two North/Bob rows (800 and 400). It computes 1200+800+600+400 = 3000 instead of 2100.

tasks.handCheck: Nine data rows, tested against Region=North AND Rep=Alice. r2 North/Alice 1200 IN. r3 North/Bob OUT (rep). r4 South/Alice OUT (region). r5 North/Alice 600 IN. r6 East/Carol OUT (both). r7 North/Bob OUT (rep). r8 South/Bob OUT (both). r9 North/Alice 300 IN. r10 East/Alice OUT (region). 1200 + 600 + 300 = 2100. All addends are integers below 2^53, so the sum is exact in binary64 regardless of accumulation order.

tasks.intent: In the order table in A1:C10, count how many rows have a Belopp that is STRICTLY greater than 1000 (a Belopp of exactly 1000 does not count) AND a Status of Skickad. Put the count in E2.

distractor.why: It applies only the amount test and never looks at Status, so it also counts the two Makulerad rows over 1000 (2000 and 1100). It computes 6 instead of 4.

tasks.handCheck: Nine data rows against Belopp>1000 AND Status=Skickad. r2 1500 Skickad IN. r3 900 fails amount OUT. r4 2000 but Makulerad OUT. r5 1000 is NOT strictly greater than 1000 OUT. r6 1200 Skickad IN. r7 3000 Skickad IN. r8 1100 but Makulerad OUT. r9 800 Makulerad OUT (fails both). r10 2500 Skickad IN. Count = 4 (rows 2, 6, 7, 10). Row 5 is the boundary tooth: with ">=1000" the answer would be 5, so strict-versus-inclusive is measurable and is named in the intent.

tasks.intent: In the product list in A1:B9, add up the Units for every product whose code begins with the prefix WID- (the hyphen is part of the prefix). A code such as WIDGET, which starts with WID but has no hyphen, must NOT be included, and neither must a code that merely contains WID- somewhere later, such as TWID-500. Put the total in D2.

distractor.why: Dropping the hyphen from the pattern widens it: WID* also matches WIDGET, so the 25 units of WIDGET are added. It computes 50+40+20+25 = 135 instead of 110.

tasks.handCheck: Calcula anchors a wildcard pattern to the WHOLE cell text — xlookup_wildcard_match_recursive returns ti == text.len() when the pattern is exhausted — so "WID-*" means exactly 'starts with WID-'. r2 WID-100 matches -> 50. r3 GAD-200 no. r4 WID-205 matches -> 40. r5 WIDGET: pattern needs '-' at index 3, text has 'G' -> no match. r6 GAD-310 no. r7 WID-410 matches -> 20. r8 TWID-500: pattern needs 'W' at index 0, text has 'T', and the pattern has no leading star to skip it -> no match. r9 GAD-999 no. 50 + 40 + 20 = 110, exact in binary64.

tasks.intent: In the timesheet in A1:C10, work out the average Hours across the rows where the Employee is Anna AND the Department is Support, and round that average to 2 decimal places. Put the rounded average in E2.

distractor.why: The single-condition AVERAGEIF averages ALL of Anna's rows, including her two Sales rows (8 and 3). It computes (7+8+8+8+3)/5 = 34/5 = 6.8 instead of 7.67.

tasks.handCheck: Rows with Employee=Anna AND Department=Support: r2 (7), r6 (8), r8 (8). Excluded: Anna's Sales rows r4 (8) and r10 (3); Support rows belonging to someone else, r5 Cara (9) and r7 Ben (5); and r3 Ben/Sales (6), r9 Cara/Sales (4) which fail both. Sum = 23, count = 3, average = 23/3. In binary64 23.0/3.0 = 7.666666666666667. ROUND is implemented as (num * 10^digits).round() / 10^digits (fn_round, core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:4899-4920), so: 7.666666666666667 * 100 = 766.6666666666667, .round() = 767.0, 767.0/100.0 = 7.67. IEEE division is correctly rounded, so 767.0/100.0 is the nearest double to the real 7.67, which is bit-identical to what the literal 7.67 parses to. Confirmed by executing the exact double chain: the equality test 767/100 === 7.67 is true. Rounding direction is also load-bearing here: truncating to 2 decimals would give 7.66, so ROUND versus ROUNDDOWN is measurable.

tasks.intent: In the sales table in A1:C9, find the largest single Amount among the rows where the Region is West AND the Channel is Online. Rows in another region, and West rows sold through the Retail channel, must be ignored even when their Amount is bigger. Put the result in E2.

distractor.why: The one-condition version keeps every West row regardless of channel, so the West/Retail row of 6100 wins. It computes 6100 instead of 5300.

tasks.handCheck: Rows with Region=West AND Channel=Online: r2 (4200), r5 (5300), r7 (3100). max(4200, 5300, 3100) = 5300. The three decoys are deliberately larger: r3 East/Online 9500 is the global column maximum but the wrong region; r4 West/Retail 6100 is the maximum among West rows but the wrong channel; r6 North/Online 7000 is the maximum among Online rows but the wrong region. So MAX over the column (9500), MAXIFS on Region alone (6100) and MAXIFS on Channel alone (9500) all miss 5300. Every Amount is an integer, exact in binary64, and there are no ties.

tasks.intent: Column A holds SKUs, column B the product name and column C the price. Look up the SKU "SKU-107" with an exact match and return its price from column C. The match must be exact, so the similar code SKU-1070 in the list does not count as a match. Because SKU-107 itself is not in the list, the formula must return the text "Not found" (spelled exactly that way) instead of an error.

distractor.why: VLOOKUP has no if_not_found argument. With range_lookup FALSE the exact-match scan of the first column finds neither "SKU-107" nor an equal to it ("SKU-1070" is a different string), so fn_vlookup falls off the end of its loop and returns #N/A, not the text "Not found" the request asks for. The other reflex, =VLOOKUP("SKU-107",A2:C7,3,TRUE), is worse: the approximate branch keeps the last row whose key compares <= the target and so returns a neighbouring row's price silently instead of the fallback.

tasks.handCheck: Lookup array A2:A7 = SKU-100, SKU-101, SKU-102, SKU-103, SKU-104, SKU-1070. XLOOKUP's match_mode defaults to 0 (exact); exactness goes through Self::exact_lookup_equal -> excel_comparison_ordering, which compares text as text, so "SKU-107" is not equal to "SKU-1070" (different strings) nor to any other entry. found_index is None. args.len() is 4 > 3, so the None arm evaluates args[3], the literal "Not found", and returns it (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:5540-5550 on the scan path, and the identical None arm at 5501-5507 on the lookup-cache fast path, so both spellings agree). Result = the text Not found.

tasks.intent: Column A lists the minimum quantity that starts each volume-discount tier and column B the discount percent for that tier. For an order of 75 units, return the discount percent for the band the order falls into, that is the row with the highest minimum quantity that is not above 75. 75 is not itself a listed threshold. Return the number as it stands in column B (10 meaning ten percent), not a fraction.

distractor.why: FALSE forces an exact match, but 75 is not one of the listed thresholds (0, 10, 50, 100, 250). fn_vlookup's exact branch scans the first column with exact_lookup_equal, matches nothing, and returns #N/A instead of 10. Reaching for exact match on a banded table is the standard reflex error; so is =XLOOKUP(75,A2:A6,B2:B6,"",1), which takes the next LARGER threshold, 100, and answers 15.

tasks.handCheck: Thresholds in A2:A6 are 0, 10, 50, 100, 250; returns in B2:B6 are 0, 5, 10, 15, 20. The reference passes -1 in the 5th positional slot, which the catalogue confirms is match_mode. fn_xlookup (evaluator.rs:5518-5523) dispatches match_mode -1 to xlookup_approx_smaller (evaluator.rs:5843-5877). That helper first tries an exact match: 75 is absent, so None. It then walks the whole array keeping the LARGEST number strictly less than 75: 0 (best), 10 (larger, best), 50 (larger, best), 100 (not < 75, skipped), 250 (skipped). best_index = 2 (0-based). return_array[2] = B4 = 10. Note the fast path is not taken here because it is gated on match_mode == 0 (evaluator.rs:5464), so only the scan path runs. Result = 10, an integer and therefore exact in binary floating point. The if_not_found "" is a positional placeholder needed to reach match_mode and never fires.

tasks.intent: The table has region names down column A and the quarter headings Q1 to Q4 across row 1, with the sales figures in B2:E5. Return the sales figure for the region East in quarter Q3, matching both the region name and the quarter heading exactly, so that the formula still finds the right cell if the quarter columns are reordered.

distractor.why: A hard-coded col_index_num counts columns from the left edge of table_array, so 3 is column C (Q2), not column D (Q3). fn_vlookup finds "East" in the first column at row 3 and returns row[2] = C4 = 210, not 190. It is a silent wrong number rather than an error, which is exactly why the wrong-column-index reflex survives review; it also cannot follow the heading if the quarter columns are reordered.

tasks.handCheck: MATCH("East",A2:A5,0): the array is North, South, East, West; fn_match's match_type 0 branch (evaluator.rs:8519-8538) returns i+1 for the first exact hit, so 3. MATCH("Q3",B1:E1,0): the array is Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4, so 3. INDEX(B2:E5,3,3): the literal rectangle B2:E5 has rows=4, cols=4, and args.len()==3 so one_index is false and cols>1, giving flat_idx = row_num*cols + col_num = 2*4 + 2 = 10 (both indices are 0-based after the -1 at evaluator.rs:8403-8414). 10 < 16, so no #REF!. r = min_row + 10/4 = row(B2) + 2 = row 4; c = min_col + 10%4 = col B + 2 = col D. The cell is D4 = 190, an integer and exact in binary floating point.

tasks.intent: The staff list has the employee name in column A and the badge number in column B. Return the name of the employee whose badge number is exactly 4126. The answer sits to the LEFT of the badge column.

distractor.why: VLOOKUP always searches the FIRST column of table_array, which here is the name column A. Its exact branch compares with exact_lookup_equal, which routes through excel_comparison_ordering; a number and a text value are different classes and are never equal (the same rule that makes ="1"=1 FALSE, evaluator.rs:2800-2816), so the number 4126 matches no name and the formula returns #N/A rather than Carla Nyman. VLOOKUP structurally cannot return a value to the left of its key.

tasks.handCheck: MATCH(4126,B2:B6,0): B2:B6 holds the numbers 4102, 4118, 4126, 4133, 4140; fn_match's exact branch (evaluator.rs:8519-8538) returns i+1 at the first exact_lookup_equal hit, which is the third entry, so 3. INDEX(A2:A6,3): A2:A6 is a literal rectangle with rows=5, cols=1, and args.len()==2 so one_index is true. Because cols<=1 the flat index is just row_num = 2 (0-based), well under rows*cols = 5, giving r = row(A2) + 2/1 = row 4 and c = col A + 2%1 = col A. That is A4 = "Carla Nyman" (evaluator.rs:8420-8431; the cols<=1 branch is the documented reading-order rule for a one-dimensional array). The four other rows - badges 4102, 4118, 4133, 4140 - are all excluded. Result = the text Carla Nyman.

tasks.intent: Column C holds the status of each task log entry. Return the position of the LAST entry whose status is Open, searching from the bottom of the list upward, counting the first data row (row 2) as position 1. Two entries are Open, and the later one is the answer. Return the position number itself, not the date or the task name.

distractor.why: MATCH has no search-direction argument (its third argument is match_type, not a direction), so fn_match always scans first to last and stops at the FIRST Open, C3, returning 2 instead of 4. The same wrong answer comes from writing =XMATCH("Open",C2:C6,0) and omitting the search_mode of -1, since fn_xmatch defaults search_mode to 1.

tasks.handCheck: C2:C6 is Closed, Open, Closed, Open, Closed at positions 1 to 5. fn_xmatch (evaluator.rs:14424-14452) builds its scan order from search_mode: -1 gives (0..len).rev(), i.e. 4, 3, 2, 1, 0 zero-based. match_mode 0 takes the exact branch. The lookup value "Open" is text so lookup_num is None, and the number-vs-number arm of the condition cannot fire; the else-if compares lookup_text to val.as_text(). i=4 is C6 "Closed", no match. i=3 is C5 "Open", match, and the function returns (i+1) = 4. Result = 4, an integer and exact. The first Open, at position 2, is the value that must be excluded - and it is exactly what the distractor returns, so the two are distinguishable.

tasks.intent: In H2, count the working days for the Site survey task in row 2: from its start date 2025-04-01 in B2 through its due date 2025-04-30 in C2, counting both of those days themselves, treating every Saturday and Sunday as a non-working day, and also skipping the public holidays listed in F2:F4.

distractor.why: It drops the third argument, so the holiday list is never applied: it removes only the 8 weekend days and answers 22 instead of 20 (measured). The plainer wrong idiom =C2-B2 answers 29 (calendar days, and one short because it does not count the start day), and =C2-B2+1 answers 30.

tasks.handCheck: Re-derived independently of the author. The grader seeds "2025-04-01" as a serial via seed_value -> date_serial::parse_date_string (core/calcula-format/src/ai/formula_verify.rs:192, core/engine/src/date_serial.rs:205), so B2 = 45748 and C2 = 45777; the inclusive window is all 30 days of April 2025. date_serial::weekday is ((serial-1) mod 7) with 0 = Sunday (date_serial.rs:136), so 45748 -> (45747 mod 7) = 2 = Tuesday and 45777 -> 3 = Wednesday. Saturdays inside: 04-05, 04-12, 04-19, 04-26; Sundays: 04-06, 04-13, 04-20, 04-27 -- 8 weekend days, leaving 30-8 = 22. Of the three holidays, F2 = 45765 = 2025-04-18 (WEEKDAY(...,2) = 5, Friday) and F3 = 45768 = 2025-04-21 (WEEKDAY(...,2) = 1, Monday) both lie inside the window on weekdays and each removes one day; F4 = 2025-05-01 lies outside and removes nothing. 22 - 2 = 20. CONFIRMED by running the fixture through the real grader (calcula_format::ai::formula_verify::evaluate_fixture over core/engine): reference = 20, =NETWORKDAYS(B2,C2) = 22, =C2-B2 = 29, =C2-B2+1 = 30, and the decoy row =NETWORKDAYS(B3,C3,F2:F4) = 15.

tasks.intent: In D2, work out how many COMPLETE years Anna Lind has been employed, from her hire date 2018-09-15 in B2 up to the as-of date 2025-06-30 in B7. Count only whole years: an anniversary that the as-of date has not yet reached does not count, so a part-year is dropped rather than rounded.

distractor.why: Subtracting calendar years ignores the month and day, so it counts the 2025 anniversary that has not happened yet and answers 7 instead of 6 (measured). The fixture is chosen so the two disagree: Anna's anniversary (15 September) falls AFTER the 30 June as-of date. Picking Bjorn Ek's row instead would have hidden the bug -- his March anniversary has already passed, and both formulas measure 5 there.

tasks.handCheck: Re-derived independently. B2 seeds to the serial for 2018-09-15 and B7 to 2025-06-30 (formula_verify::seed_value -> date_serial::parse_date_string). fn_datedif (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:8214) converts both back with serial_to_date and calls date_serial::datedif_years (date_serial.rs:187), which is: years = ey - sy, then subtract one if em < sm or (em == sm and ed < sd). Here ey-sy = 2025-2018 = 7, and em = 6 is less than sm = 9, so one year is dropped: 6. The distractor is a plain calendar-year subtraction with no month test, so it keeps the 7. CONFIRMED against the real grader over this exact fixture: =DATEDIF(B2,B7,"Y") = 6, =YEAR(B7)-YEAR(B2) = 7, and the three decoy rows now measure 5 (B3), 9 (B4) and 4 (B5) -- all distinct from 6.

tasks.intent: In E2, count how many of the orders in B2:B8 were placed in March 2025, that is with an order date from 2025-03-01 to 2025-03-31 inclusive. Orders dated in March of any other year must not be counted.

distractor.why: The one-condition version tests the month only, so it also counts SO-103 dated 2024-03-19 and answers 4 instead of 3 (measured). March of a different year is exactly the row this fixture plants to catch it.

tasks.handCheck: Walk the seven dates: 2025-03-04 counts; 2025-02-28 is February, out; 2024-03-19 is March but 2024, out; 2025-03-17 counts; 2025-04-01 is one day past the window, out; 2025-03-31 counts (the inclusive upper bound); 2025-01-15 out. Three rows qualify. YEAR and MONTH are both on the array-lift allowlist (BuiltinFunction::Year at core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:3037 and ::Month at 3038, inside lifts_over_arrays at evaluator.rs:2945), so each returns an array over the range; the comparison yields a boolean array, TRUE coerces to 1 in EvalResult::as_number (evaluator.rs:641), and SUMPRODUCT sums the elementwise product. CONFIRMED against the real grader over this exact fixture: reference = 3, one-condition distractor = 4, the equivalent =COUNTIFS(B2:B8,">="&DATE(2025,3,1),B2:B8,"<="&DATE(2025,3,31)) = 3, and the trailing-*1 spelling =SUMPRODUCT((YEAR(B2:B8)=2025)*(MONTH(B2:B8)=3)*1) = 3.

tasks.intent: In E3, work out how many days there are from the invoice date of invoice F-2002 (2025-02-10, in B3) to its due date, where the due date is the last day of the month AFTER the invoice month. Report the difference as a plain whole number of days -- the due date minus the invoice date, with the invoice date itself counting as day zero -- not as a date.

distractor.why: Passing 0 months takes the end of the invoice's OWN month (2025-02-28) instead of the month after it, answering 18 instead of 49 (measured). Two further wrong idioms also fail on this fixture: =DAY(EOMONTH(B3,1)) answers 31 -- the length of March, not the distance to it -- and =EDATE(B3,1)-B3 answers 28, stepping one month rather than to a month end.

tasks.handCheck: Re-derived independently. seed_value turns "2025-02-10" into serial 45698 (grader-confirmed by evaluating =B3). fn_eomonth (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:8172) converts to (2025,2), calls date_serial::add_months(2025,2,1,1) -> (2025,3), takes days_in_month(2025,3) = 31 and rebuilds the serial for 2025-03-31, which the grader reports as 45747 (evaluating =EOMONTH(B3,1)). 45747 - 45698 = 49. Cross-check without serials: 2025-02-10 to 2025-02-28 is 18 days (2025 is not a leap year, so February has 28), then 2025-02-28 to 2025-03-31 is 31 more; 18 + 31 = 49. CONFIRMED against the real grader over this exact fixture: reference = 49, =EOMONTH(B3,0)-B3 = 18, =DAY(EOMONTH(B3,1)) = 31, =EDATE(B3,1)-B3 = 28, and the inclusive misreading =EOMONTH(B3,1)-B3+1 = 50.

tasks.intent: In D2, count how many of the seven delivery dates in B2:B8 fall on a Saturday or a Sunday.

distractor.why: Omitting the return type leaves WEEKDAY on its default numbering (Sunday=1 .. Saturday=7), so >5 selects Friday and Saturday rather than Saturday and Sunday: it counts 2025-06-06 (Friday) and 2025-06-07 (Saturday) and answers 2 instead of 3 (measured). The fixture deliberately holds one Friday and two Sundays so the two conventions cannot agree.

tasks.handCheck: Re-derived independently, then every value confirmed cell by cell against the real engine. fn_weekday (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:8249) computes date_serial::weekday (0=Sunday..6=Saturday) and, for return_type 2, maps Sunday to 7 and every other day to its 0-based index, giving Monday=1..Sunday=7 (evaluator.rs:8258); so >5 is exactly Saturday or Sunday. Measured through the grader, one formula per cell: WEEKDAY(B2,2) = 1 (Mon), B3 = 5 (Fri), B4 = 6 (Sat), B5 = 7 (Sun), B6 = 3 (Wed), B7 = 7 (Sun), B8 = 3 (Wed). Three values exceed 5 -- B4, B5 and B7 -- so the count is 3. Under the default numbering (return_type 1, evaluator.rs:8257) those same seven days are 2, 6, 7, 1, 4, 1, 4, of which only two exceed 5. CONFIRMED against the real grader over this exact fixture: reference = 3, distractor = 2, and the equivalent =SUMPRODUCT((WEEKDAY(B2:B8,2)>=6)*1) = 3.

tasks.intent: Column B holds e-mail addresses. In E2, return only the domain part of the address in B3 — everything that comes after the @ sign, with the @ itself not included.

distractor.why: FIND returns the position OF the @ (5), so MID starts ON the @ instead of one character after it. Against this fixture it computes "@tallberg.com" — the right text with a stray leading @ — not "tallberg.com". The fix is FIND("@",B3)+1, which is exactly the off-by-one this task catches.

tasks.handCheck: AUDITOR RE-DERIVATION (author's handCheck ignored). B3 = "erik@tallberg.com". Character census: e,r,i,k = 4; @ = 1 (character 5); t,a,l,l,b,e,r,g = 8 (6-13); . = 1 (14); c,o,m = 3 (15-17). LEN(B3) = 17, and there is exactly one @, at character 5. TEXTAFTER(text, delimiter) with instance_num defaulted to 1 returns text[positions[0] + delimiter.len()..] — read at core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:11676 — i.e. everything strictly after the first @, which is characters 6..17 = "tallberg.com". Matches expectText. DISTRACTOR RE-DERIVATION: FIND("@",B3) = 5 (fn_find at core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:7766 returns a 1-based CHARACTER position via byte_offset_to_char_pos at line 154). LEN(B3) = 17. fn_mid (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:5249) converts start 5 to a 0-based skip of 4, then takes 17 characters, so it yields "@tallberg.com" (13 characters). Different from the reference, so the task discriminates. OTHER WRONG ROUTES CHECKED: =TEXTAFTER(B3,".") = "com" (fails); =TEXTBEFORE(B3,"@") = "erik" (fails). Teeth: B2 and B4 end in @nordvind.se and B5 in @kvarnby.no, so no other row can produce "tallberg.com" — a misread row is visible. Result is pure text, so no floating-point question arises.

tasks.intent: Column B holds locations written as comma-separated parts, always ending with the country, but the NUMBER of parts varies from row to row — some rows are "City, Region, Country" and some carry an extra district part. In E2, return the country from B3 — that is, the part after the LAST comma, whichever comma that turns out to be — with any leading or trailing spaces removed.

distractor.why: With no instance argument TEXTAFTER takes the FIRST comma, and it also keeps the space that follows it. Against this fixture it computes " Sentrum, Viken, Norway" — three parts glued together behind a leading space — instead of "Norway". A second tempting near-miss now fails too: because B3 carries THREE commas while the other rows carry two, the "count from the front" guess =TRIM(TEXTAFTER(B3,",",2)) returns "Viken, Norway", so only the negative instance -1 (count from the end) is right. The TRIM is separately load-bearing: without it the answer is " Norway" with a leading space.

tasks.handCheck: AUDITOR RE-DERIVATION (fixture changed by the audit; author's handCheck superseded). B3 = "Oslo, Sentrum, Viken, Norway". Character census: O,s,l,o = 1-4; "," = 5; space+S,e,n,t,r,u,m = 6-13; "," = 14; space+V,i,k,e,n = 15-20; "," = 21; space+N,o,r,w,a,y = 22-28. LEN = 28, and there are exactly THREE commas, at 5, 14 and 21. fn_textafter (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:11676) collects positions with match_indices, and for a negative instance uses idx = -instance-1 = 0 and pos = positions[positions.len()-1-idx] = positions[2] = the LAST comma; it returns text[pos + delimiter.len()..] = everything after character 21 = " Norway" (one space then six letters). fn_trim (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:5125 — NOT 11611, which the author cited in error) does split_whitespace().join(" "), which strips both ends, giving "Norway". Matches expectText. DISTRACTOR RE-DERIVATION: =TEXTAFTER(B3,",") defaults to instance 1, positions[0] = 5, returns " Sentrum, Viken, Norway" — plainly different. SECOND NEAR-MISS RE-DERIVED: =TRIM(TEXTAFTER(B3,",",2)) takes positions[1] = 14, returns " Viken, Norway", trimmed to "Viken, Norway" — also different, which is the point of giving B3 three commas. Teeth: B2 -> Sweden, B4 -> Denmark, B5 -> Finland, none equal to "Norway". The answer text is pure ASCII even though B2 carries "Göteborg"; fn_textafter indexes by byte offsets taken from match_indices, which are always character boundaries, so the non-ASCII rows are safe and in any case are not the target row.

tasks.intent: Column B holds a comma-separated list of tags for each product; the tags are separated by a single comma with no spaces and there are no empty entries. In D2, count how many tags are listed for the Headlamp in B3. The answer is a whole number of tags, not a number of commas.

distractor.why: This counts the DELIMITERS, not the items. It computes 3 (the number of commas) instead of 4 (the number of tags); n commas separate n+1 tags, so the +1 is mandatory. On B3 it returns a plausible-looking 3, which is why the intent now says outright that the answer is a count of tags and not of commas.

tasks.handCheck: AUDITOR RE-DERIVATION (author's handCheck ignored, then found to agree). B3 = "outdoor,camping,winter,safety". If the range were widened to A1:A7 / B1:B7 the by-array would contain the TEXT "Units", and compare_eval_results (evaluator.rs:9922) gives Text the sort key 1 against Number's 0, so descending order would put the header first and the anchor would be "Product" - a different answer, which is why the intent names the exclusion. tasks.intent: In D2, return the total of the points in B2:B8 after dropping the two lowest scores - the two smallest point values must be excluded from the total. All seven point values are different, so there are no ties.

distractor.why: MIN removes only ONE score, so the second lowest (11, Cecilia) is still counted: 127 - 7 = 120 instead of 109. This is the one-condition version of a two-exclusion problem and is the mistake a model makes when it reads 'drop the lowest scores' as a single MIN.

tasks.handCheck: B2:B8 = 18, 25, 11, 30, 22, 7, 14 - seven distinct integers. SUM = 18+25 = 43, +11 = 54, +30 = 84, +22 = 106, +7 = 113, +14 = 127. SMALL(B2:B8,1) = 7 (Frida, row 7) and SMALL(B2:B8,2) = 11 (Cecilia, row 4) - these are the two rows the answer must exclude. 127 - 7 - 11 = 109. Cross-check by adding the five surviving scores directly: 18 + 25 + 30 + 22 + 14 = 109. Every operand is a small integer so the result is exact in binary floating point; no rounding decision is involved. Distractor check: 127 - 7 = 120 != 109, and the gap of 11 is the second lowest score itself, so the two formulas can never coincide on this fixture.

tasks.intent: The sheet Sales lists five regions with their sales in B2:B6, and row 7 is a Total row that must not be counted in the denominator. In D2, compute North's share of the five regions' combined sales, expressed as a fraction between 0 and 1 (a tenth is written 0.1, not 10). Write it so the formula can be copied down to D3:D6 with the reference to the total staying fixed on B2:B6.

distractor.why: It lets the range run one row too far and swallows the Total row in B7. The denominator becomes 20000 + 20000 = 40000 instead of 20000, so it computes 5000/40000 = 0.125 — exactly half the right share. (The unanchored =B2/SUM(B2:B6) agrees with the reference at the anchor D2 but breaks the moment it is copied to D3, where the window slides to B3:B7 and swallows the Total row.)

tasks.handCheck: B7 is a formula, not data: SUM(B2:B6) = 5000+3000+2000+4000+6000 = 20000. North's share = B2/20000 = 5000/20000 = 1/4 = 0.25. One quarter is exact in binary floating point (2^-2), so no rounding is needed and the expectation is unambiguous. The distractor's denominator SUM(B2:B7) = 20000+20000 = 40000 gives 5000/40000 = 0.125, a different value.

tasks.intent: The sheet Revenue is a deal list in A2:C9: column A is the year, B the region, C that deal's revenue. North has two deals in 2024 and two in 2025, so North's revenue for a year must be summed across its rows, not read from one row. In E2, compute North's revenue growth from 2024 to 2025 — that is (North's total 2025 revenue minus North's total 2024 revenue) divided by North's total 2024 revenue, so 2024 is the base year. Count only the North rows and ignore South and West. Give the answer as a fraction (5% growth is 0.05, not 5), rounded to 4 decimals.

distractor.why: This is the one-condition version: it filters on the year but forgets the region, so it measures the whole company's growth instead of North's. It computes 132000/120000 - 1 = 0.1 and returns 0.1 instead of 0.125.

tasks.handCheck: North 2024 = rows 2 and 3 = 25000+15000 = 40000. North 2025 = rows 6 and 7 = 30000+15000 = 45000. Both are exact integers, so both sums are exact in binary. 45000/40000 = 1.125 = 1 + 1/8, exact; minus 1 = 0.125 = 2^-3, exact. ROUND(0.125,4): 0.125*10000 = 1250 exactly, rounds to 1250, /10000 = 0.125. Cross-check in difference form: (45000-40000)/40000 = 5000/40000 = 0.125. Distractor: 2025 total = 30000+15000+66000+21000 = 132000; 2024 total = 25000+15000+60000+20000 = 120000; 132000/120000 - 1 = 0.1 (0.10000000000000009 in doubles), rounded to 4 decimals = 0.1 — a different number. The single-cell shortcuts also fail now that North has two rows a year: C6/C2-1 = 0.2, C6/C3-1 = 1, C7/C2-1 = -0.4, C7/C3-1 = 0, none of them 0.125.

tasks.intent: The sheet Products lists products in A2:D5 with a status in column B, revenue in column C and cost in column D. In F2, compute the gross margin across the ACTIVE products only: (total active revenue minus total active cost) divided by total active revenue. Any row whose status is Discontinued must be left out of both totals. Give the answer as a fraction of revenue (a 40% margin is 0.4, not 40), rounded to 4 decimals.

distractor.why: It ignores the Status column and folds the Discontinued Relic row into both totals. Relic is a near-zero-margin line (6000 revenue against 5900 cost), so it drags the ratio down: the distractor computes 5100/22000 = 0.231818..., returning 0.2318 instead of 0.3125.

tasks.intent: The sheet Channels lists marketing channels in A2:C5 with visits in column B and orders in column C. In E4, compute the Social row's conversion rate — Social's orders divided by Social's visits — as a fraction rounded to 4 decimals. Social's visit tracking broke, so its visits are recorded as 0 while 3 orders were still attributed to it: the division cannot be done, and in that case the formula must return the text n/a (lower case, exactly those three characters) instead of letting a division error show. The answer is about the Social row alone, not about the site as a whole.

distractor.why: The unguarded division is exactly what the intent forbids. B4 holds the number 0, so the evaluator's divide arm returns CellError::Div0 (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:2604) and the cell shows #DIV/0! rather than the required text n/a. =ROUND(C4/B4,4) fails the same way, merely turning one error into another. The inverted =IFERROR(ROUND(B4/C4,4),"n/a") now fails too: 0/3 is a perfectly good 0, so it returns the number 0 instead of n/a.

tasks.handCheck: B4 = 0 (visits) and C4 = 3 (orders). The divide arm tests the divisor first — core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:2604, `(Some(_), Some(r)) if r == 0.0 => EvalResult::Error(CellError::Div0)` — so C4/B4 = 3/0 is #DIV/0!. ROUND then calls as_number() on that error, which returns None for EvalResult::Error (evaluator.rs:638-660), so ROUND yields #VALUE!; either way IFERROR's first argument is an Error, so fn_iferror (evaluator.rs:6666-6670) evaluates its second argument and the cell holds the string n/a. The result is text and depends on no floating-point value at all. Positive control that the fixture is well formed: the same formula on the Search row would be ROUND(500/4000,4) = ROUND(0.125,4) = 0.125, so the guard is the only thing standing between the target and an error. An equally correct alternative a model may write is =IF(B4=0,"n/a",ROUND(C4/B4,4)), which also returns n/a. Making orders 3 rather than 0 is what gives operand order teeth: with 0 orders the inverted B4/C4 was also 0/0 and also returned n/a; with 3 orders it returns the number 0 and fails.

tasks.intent: The sheet Orders lists sales reps in A2:C6 with each rep's region in column A and amount in column C; the North rows are not next to each other. In E3, compute Ben's amount as a share of the North region's total amount only — not of all regions' amounts. Give the answer as a fraction between 0 and 1 (a fifth is written 0.2, not 20), rounded to 4 decimals.

distractor.why: It divides by the grand total of every region instead of by North's own subtotal, so the two South rows (Clara 4000 and Erik 6000) inflate the denominator from 16000 to 26000. It returns 5000/26000 = 0.192307..., i.e. 0.1923 instead of 0.3125. Summing C2:C3 to get "the North rows above" fails too, because David's North row sits below a South row at row 5.

tasks.handCheck: The criteria A3 reads as the text North (case-insensitive exact match in the engine's criteria matcher). SUMIF(A2:A6,"North",C2:C6) picks rows 2, 3 and 5: 3000+5000+8000 = 16000; the South rows 4 and 6 are excluded. Ben's share = C3/16000 = 5000/16000 = 5/16 = 0.3125, exact in binary. ROUND(0.3125,4) = 0.3125, and the stated 4 decimals has teeth since ROUND(0.3125,2) would be 0.31. Distractor: SUM(C2:C6) = 3000+5000+4000+8000+6000 = 26000, and 5000/26000 = 0.1923076..., rounded to 0.1923 — clearly different.

tasks.intent: In D2, return the letter grade for the score in B2 using four bands: "A" when the score is 90 or higher, "B" when it is 80 or higher but below 90, "C" when it is 70 or higher but below 80, and "F" for anything below 70. The band edges are inclusive at the bottom: a score of exactly 90 is an A, exactly 80 is a B, and exactly 70 is a C. Return the letter as text.

distractor.why: The single-IF, two-band version collapses everything under 90 into "B". B2 is 70, so it returns "B", not "C". The second common miss, =IF(B2>90,"A",IF(B2>80,"B",IF(B2>70,"C","F"))), uses strict > at every edge and drops the exact 70 through to the catch-all, returning "F". Both wrong classes - the dropped band and the strict boundary - are caught by this one target cell, which is why B2 sits exactly on a band edge.

tasks.handCheck: Re-derived independently. B2 holds the number 70. IFS evaluates condition/value pairs left to right: pair 1, 70>=90 -> FALSE; pair 2, 70>=80 -> FALSE; pair 3, 70>=70 -> TRUE, so IFS returns the paired value "C" and never evaluates the fourth pair. Result = "C". The argument count is 8 (even), which fn_ifs requires (evaluator.rs:6678 rejects an odd count with #VALUE!), and the bare TRUE is lexed as a boolean literal (lexer.rs:463), not as a name, so the catch-all parses. Rows that must give a DIFFERENT answer: B3=92 -> "A", B4=90 -> "A" (top boundary), B5=80 -> "B" (middle boundary), B6=69 -> "F", B7=55 -> "F". Rows 6 and 7 are the excluded rows: they are the only ones falling to the bottom band.

tasks.intent: In F2, return TRUE or FALSE for the order in row 2 answering whether it qualifies for the regional bonus. It qualifies only when all three of these hold: the Region in B2 is North, the Amount in C2 is at least 5000 (an amount of exactly 5000 qualifies), and the Returned flag in D2 is anything other than the text Yes. If any one of the three fails, return FALSE.

distractor.why: The two-condition version of a three-condition problem. Region and amount both pass on row 2, so AND(TRUE,TRUE) returns TRUE instead of the required FALSE. Row 2 is built so the Returned flag is the ONLY failing test, which is exactly what makes a dropped third condition visible. The Google-Sheets/VBA-flavoured miss =IF(B2="North" AND C2>=5000,...) does not parse at all in Calcula, since AND is a function, never an infix keyword.

tasks.handCheck: Re-derived independently. Row 2: B2 is the text "North", so B2="North" is TRUE. C2 is the number 5000 and 5000>=5000 is TRUE (the inclusive edge the intent states). D2 is the text "Yes", so D2<>"Yes" is FALSE. fn_and (evaluator.rs:4827) short-circuits on the first Some(false) and returns Boolean(false). Result = FALSE. Teeth: row 3 (North, 8000, No) satisfies all three and returns TRUE, so any wrong-row reference yields the opposite answer; row 4 fails on region, row 5 fails on amount (4000 < 5000), row 6 fails on region. Row 3 is the row a correct answer must NOT be read from.

tasks.intent: In D2, translate the one-letter status code in B2 into words: A means "Approved", P means "Pending", R means "Rejected", and any code that is none of those three must come out as the text "Unknown" rather than an error. Return the word as text.

distractor.why: Omitting the trailing default is the classic SWITCH mistake. With six arguments after the expression the count is EVEN, so fn_switch (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:6692) computes has_default = false, matches nothing, and returns CellError::NA - the cell shows #N/A, not the required text "Unknown". A second likely miss, =IF(B2="A","Approved",IF(B2="P","Pending",IF(B2="R","Rejected"))), leaves the innermost IF without a false branch and returns FALSE rather than "Unknown".

tasks.handCheck: Re-derived independently. B2 holds the text "X". fn_switch evaluates the expression, then walks the remaining arguments as pairs: pairs.len() = 7, odd, so has_default = true and pair_count = 7/2 = 3. Pair 1 compares "X" with "A" via exact_lookup_equal (evaluator.rs:2800) - not equal; pair 2 "X" vs "P" - not equal; pair 3 "X" vs "R" - not equal. No match, so it evaluates pairs.last(), the seventh entry, and returns "Unknown". Teeth: rows 3-6 all carry codes that DO hit a pair (A, P, R, A), so a formula reading the wrong row returns "Approved", "Pending" or "Rejected". Row 2 is the only row that exercises the default branch, which is precisely the branch the intent pins.

tasks.intent: In D2, return TRUE if the quantity in B2 has reached a stock limit and FALSE otherwise. A quantity counts as having reached a limit when it is at or below the reorder point of 10, or at or above the storage cap of 100. Both endpoints count as reaching the limit: a quantity of exactly 10 returns TRUE and a quantity of exactly 100 returns TRUE. A quantity strictly between 10 and 100 returns FALSE.

distractor.why: The strict-inequality reading of "outside 10 to 100" is the single most likely miss, and it excludes the endpoints the intent explicitly includes. With B2=100: 100<10 is FALSE and 100>100 is FALSE, so OR returns FALSE instead of TRUE. The one-condition version =B2<=10 also fails on this row (100<=10 is FALSE -> FALSE), so the target cell catches both the boundary error AND a dropped disjunct. The inverted form =NOT(AND(B2>10,B2<100)) happens to return TRUE here, so it is not the distractor of record.

tasks.handCheck: Re-derived independently. B2 = 100. First disjunct: 100<=10 is FALSE. Second disjunct: 100>=100 is TRUE. fn_or (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:4848) returns Boolean(true) on the first Some(true) operand. Result = TRUE. Teeth - rows the correct answer must EXCLUDE: B3=55 -> OR(FALSE,FALSE)=FALSE and B5=99 -> OR(FALSE,FALSE)=FALSE, both strictly inside the limits. Rows that also flag: B4=8 (at or below 10) -> TRUE, B6=10 (the lower endpoint, inclusive) -> TRUE, B7=120 -> TRUE. B5=99 is deliberately one below the cap so an off-by-one cap of >=99 would wrongly flag it.

tasks.intent: In D2, compute the commission on the sale amount in B2 using three tiers applied to the whole amount: 10% of the amount when it is 10000 or more, 5% of the amount when it is 5000 or more but under 10000, and 2% of the amount when it is under 5000. The tier edges are inclusive at the bottom, so an amount of exactly 10000 gets 10% and an amount of exactly 5000 gets 5%. The rate applies to the entire amount, not just the part above the tier edge. Round the commission to 2 decimals.

distractor.why: The two-tier version drops the middle 5% band, so everything under 10000 is paid at 2%. With B2=5000 it computes 5000*0.02 = 100 instead of 250. The other likely miss, strict > at both edges - =ROUND(IF(B2>10000,B2*0.1,IF(B2>5000,B2*0.05,B2*0.02)),2) - pushes exactly 5000 down into the 2% band and also returns 100. A progressive/marginal reading, paying 2% on the first 5000 and 5% only above it, would return 100 as well. All three wrong readings land on 100, cleanly distinct from 250.

tasks.handCheck: Re-derived independently. B2 = 5000. Outer test 5000>=10000 -> FALSE, so the false branch (the inner IF) is taken. Inner test 5000>=5000 -> TRUE (the stated inclusive edge), so the value is 5000*0.05. Floating point check, because the corpus rules forbid guessing one: 0.05 as an IEEE-754 double is 0.05000000000000000277555756156289135..., and 5000 times that is 250.0000000000000138777878078..., an excess of 1.3878e-14 over 250. The ULP at magnitude 250 is 2^-45 = 2.8422e-14, so half a ULP is 1.4211e-14. The excess is smaller than half a ULP, so the product rounds to exactly 250.0 - the multiplication is exact in the result. ROUND(250,2) then computes (250*100).round()/100 = 25000/100 = 250 (fn_round, evaluator.rs:4899). Result = 250 exactly. Teeth: B3=12000 -> 1200, B4=9000 -> 450, B5=4000 -> 80, B6=10000 -> 1000 (top boundary). Every other row yields a different number, so no wrong-row reference can land on 250 by accident, and B5 is the excluded bottom-tier row.

tasks.intent: Cell E4 must show the revenue per unit for the product on row 4: the revenue in B4 divided by the units in C4. If the unit count is zero that division is a #DIV/0! error, and in that case E4 must show the number 0 instead of the error.

distractor.why: The Google Sheets one-argument form, where an omitted second argument means "return blank on error". Calcula's IFERROR is strictly binary: fn_iferror opens with `if args.len() != 2 { return EvalResult::Error(CellError::Value); }` (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:6666-6667), so E4 shows #VALUE! rather than the number 0. Note the arity check runs BEFORE the inner expression is even looked at, so this spelling fails on every row, not just the erroring one. The bare unguarded =B4/C4 fails differently but just as visibly, showing #DIV/0!.

tasks.handCheck: Re-derived independently. B4 = 500, C4 = 0. The / operator goes through eval_divide, whose FIRST match arm is `(Some(_), Some(r)) if r == 0.0 => EvalResult::Error(CellError::Div0)` (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:2602-2604), so argument 1 of IFERROR is Error(Div0). fn_iferror (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:6666-6670) has arity 2, tests `matches!(val, EvalResult::Error(_))` -> true, and evaluates argument 2, the numeric literal 0, returning Number(0.0). IFERROR is on both the `lifts_over_arrays` list and the `inspects_errors` allowlist (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:3034-3035 and 3153-3154), so the generic error-propagation gate does NOT intercept the error before the function sees it - this is the exact case that allowlist exists for. Expected value: exactly 0, an integer, exact in binary floating point. Teeth: every other row divides cleanly to the SAME number - 1200/40 = 30, 900/30 = 30, 750/25 = 30 - so any off-by-one row reference returns 30, never 0, and an unguarded division on the correct row returns an error rather than a number.

tasks.intent: Cell D2 must show the price for SKU S900, taken from the SKU/price list in A2:B5 with an EXACT-match lookup. When the SKU is not present in the list the lookup produces #N/A, and that #N/A must be replaced by the text Not stocked. Replace only the not-found #N/A - any other kind of error must still show through.

distractor.why: Dropping the fourth argument makes range_lookup default to TRUE (`} else { true }`, core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:15996-15998), so VLOOKUP takes its APPROXIMATE branch instead of the exact one. Text keys order through text_cmp::cmp_ci (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:16303-16309): "S900" and "S103" agree on 'S' and diverge at the second character, where '9' outranks '1', so "S900" sorts above every key in the column. The approximate walk keeps the LAST key that is <= the needle, which is row 5, and returns column 2 of it: the number 60, the price of S103. Both code paths agree on this - the legacy scan sets best_idx to the final row, and the cached path's rightmost_le_text lands on the same index - so the answer does not depend on whether a lookup-cache pass is active. No #N/A is ever raised, IFNA never fires, and D2 shows a plausible wrong PRICE instead of "Not stocked": a silent wrong answer, the worst failure mode this family exists to catch.

tasks.handCheck: Re-derived independently. VLOOKUP("S900", A2:B5, 2, FALSE): the bare token FALSE lexes to Token::Boolean(false) (core/parser/src/lexer.rs:465), so range_lookup is false and fn_vlookup (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:15946) takes the exact-match branch. "S900" contains no * or ?, so wildcard_pattern returns None and each first-column key is tested with exact_lookup_equal against S100, S101, S102, S103. None is equal, the loop falls through, and the function returns EvalResult::Error(CellError::NA). (A2:B5 is 4 rows x 2 columns so the PERF-03 fast rect is eligible; its exact path calls ExactIndex::first_match, which also finds nothing and yields the identical CellError::NA, so both paths agree.) fn_ifna (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:6672-6676) tests specifically `matches!(val, EvalResult::Error(CellError::NA))`, which holds, and evaluates argument 2, returning Text("Not stocked") - spelled exactly as the intent states, capital N, lowercase s. IFNA is on the inspects_errors allowlist (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:3154) so the generic propagation gate does not swallow the #N/A before the function sees it. Teeth: the four prices are all different (25, 40, 15, 60), so a lookup that silently lands on a neighbouring row returns a distinguishable number rather than anything resembling the fallback text.

tasks.intent: Cell E2 must show what an UNGUARDED exact-match lookup returns when a code is not in the catalogue. Look up SKU S900 in the code column A2:A5 and return the matching price from C2:C5. Give the lookup NO not-found argument and wrap it in NO error handling of any kind, so that when the code is missing the cell displays the error the lookup itself produces rather than any substitute value.

distractor.why: The reflex of supplying a fallback the intent explicitly forbids. With a fourth argument present, `args.len() > 3` holds at the None arm of fn_xlookup (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:5541-5548, and identically in the cached branch at 5500-5506), so instead of EvalResult::Error(CellError::NA) the function evaluates argument 4 and returns Text("Not found"). E2 then holds text, not the #N/A the expectation requires, and the task's whole point - that an unguarded miss must SHOW its error - goes untested. A second, sloppier spelling fails too: =VLOOKUP("S900",A2:C5,3) omits range_lookup, defaults to TRUE, and its approximate walk keeps the last row because "S900" outranks every key by cmp_ci, returning the number 9 (Screw's price) - a plausible wrong price where an error was required.

tasks.handCheck: Re-derived independently. fn_xlookup (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:5409) accepts 3 to 6 arguments. With exactly 3, match_mode defaults to 0 (exact) because `args.len() > 4` is false, and search_mode defaults to 1 because `args.len() > 5` is false. xlookup_exact scans the flattened A2:A5 = S100, S101, S102, S103; "S900" equals none of them, so found_index is None. At the None arm the guard `if args.len() > 3` is false, so the function returns EvalResult::Error(CellError::NA) (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:5541-5548). A2:A5 and C2:C5 are literal same-sheet 1-D vectors so the PERF-03 fast path may serve this instead; its own None arm carries the identical `if args.len() > 3 ... else Error(NA)` (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:5500-5506), so both paths return #N/A and the answer does not depend on cache state. CellError::NA renders as the literal "#N/A" (core/engine/src/cell.rs:172). Expected error literal: #N/A. Teeth: lookup_array A2:A5 and return_array C2:C5 are NOT adjacent - column B sits between them - so a model cannot get here with a two-column VLOOKUP shape, and every one of the four catalogue rows is a near miss on the same S1xx prefix.

tasks.intent: Cell D2 must count how many employees have not submitted a timesheet at all, that is, how many cells in the Hours range B2:B7 are completely EMPTY. A reported 0 is a submitted value and must NOT be counted as missing. The answer is a plain count as a number.

distractor.why: "Count the people with no hours" written as a test for zero - the exact conflation of empty and zero this task exists to catch. parse_criteria turns the numeric argument into CriteriaMatch::ExactNumber(0.0) (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:6225). matches_criteria then opens with an early return: a blank value matches ONLY the blank criteria BlankOrEmpty or OnlyBlank (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:6317-6322), so B4 and B6 - the two genuinely missing timesheets - are NOT counted. The only cell that matches is B3, Bruno's reported 0, which is a submitted value the intent explicitly excludes. The distractor returns 1 where the reference returns 2, and it gets there by counting exactly the wrong row.

tasks.handCheck: Re-derived independently. B2:B7 is a 6-row, 1-column Range, so eval_range materializes it positionally and, crucially, absent cells become EvalResult::Blank rather than Number(0.0) (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:1899-1917 and the comment above it). The six values in order are: B2 = Number(38), B3 = Number(0), B4 = Blank, B5 = Number(35), B6 = Blank, B7 = Number(42). fn_countblank (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:6592-6606) calls eval_flat, which is evaluate(...).into_flatten() (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:6415-6417) and preserves Blank entries verbatim (into_flatten_collect, core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:918-925), then counts entries where is_blank() holds, or the value is an empty Text, or an empty Array. Number(0.0) satisfies none of those - is_blank() is false for a number. Count = B4 and B6 = 2. Result Number(2.0). Expected value: exactly 2, an integer, exact in binary floating point. Teeth: Bruno's B3 = 0 MUST be excluded - it is the row that separates a real blank test from a zero test - and the three genuine entries 38, 35 and 42 must be excluded as well, so four of the six cells in the range are excluded by the correct answer.

tasks.intent: Cell D2 must answer TRUE or FALSE to one question: does the name Farid appear anywhere in the name list A2:A6? Find that name's position in the list with an exact match, then report whether a position was found - TRUE when the name is on the roster, FALSE when it is not. D2 must end up holding a boolean and must never be left showing an error.

distractor.why: The same idiom with the test inverted. MATCH still returns #N/A, and fn_iserror (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:5391-5397) answers Boolean(result.is_error()) = TRUE, so D2 says TRUE where FALSE is required. ISERROR is the exact inverse of the question in BOTH directions - TRUE for a name that is absent, FALSE for one that is present - so it is never right for either case, not merely unlucky on this fixture. NOT(ISERROR(...)) would be correct, and that missing NOT is the whole failure.

tasks.handCheck: Re-derived independently. fn_match (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:8499) with match_type 0 takes the exact branch (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:8519-8538) and walks A2:A6 = Anna, Bruno, Clara, Dinesh, Elena. "Farid" contains neither * nor ?, so the wildcard pattern is None and exact_lookup_equal is used; it matches none of the five, so the branch falls through to EvalResult::Error(CellError::NA). (A2:A6 is a literal vector so match_cached may serve it first; its match_type 0 arm builds an ExactIndex, first_match returns None, and to_result(None) yields the same Error(CellError::NA) - both paths agree, so the answer does not depend on whether a lookup-cache pass is active.) tasks.intent: In E2, use one formula to list the rep names from A2:A9 for every row where the Region in column B is North AND the Amount in column C is strictly greater than 200 (an amount of exactly 200 does not qualify). Keep the rows in their original sheet order and let the result spill down.

Row-by-row: Anna 1*0=0 EXCLUDED (120 <= 200); Hanna 1*0=0 EXCLUDED (200 is not > 200); Bjorn 0*1=0 EXCLUDED (South); Carl 1*1=1 KEPT; Diana 0*1=0 EXCLUDED (West); Erik 1*1=1 KEPT; Fatima 0*0=0 EXCLUDED; Gustav 1*1=1 KEPT. tasks.intent: In D2, use one formula that takes the product names in A2:A8, removes the duplicates so each name is kept once, and returns them sorted in descending alphabetical order (Z to A). Let the result spill down.

distractor.why: SORT's sort_order argument defaults to 1 = ascending when it is omitted (fn_sort, evaluator.rs:9830-9834), so this returns Apple, Banana, Cherry, Pear and the anchor D2 reads "Apple" instead of "Pear". The intent explicitly says Z to A, so the descending flag is pinned by the wording.

tasks.handCheck: SORTBY sorts the rows of A2:A6 by the parallel key vector C2:C6 with order -1. fn_sortby's argument walk reads args[1] as by_array1 (5 values, matching rows=5) and args[2] as a number, so order = -1 (evaluator.rs:9968-9990). Descending: 95 Nadia, 88 Quinn, 82 Omar, 71 Ivan, 60 Petra. All five keys are distinct integers, so the sort is total and no tie rule can be reached. Because the sorted array is A2:A6 only, cols==1 and the result is a flat 5-row column of NAMES, not miles. Spill = 5 rows x 1 column, anchor E2 = "Nadia". The fixture row that the answer must EXCLUDE is header row 1: including it drags the text "Miles" into the key vector, where it outranks every number under a descending sort and makes the anchor "Driver". Column B (Stops) is a decoy key whose descending order starts with Omar, not Nadia.

tasks.intent: In D2, use one formula to build a SINGLE column of shift IDs: produce as many numbers as the count in B2, starting at the First shift ID in B3 (not the Previous first ID in B5, which must be ignored) and increasing by the step in B4 for each following number. Let the result spill down.

Omitting the columns argument makes the engine read rows=B2=6, columns=B3=20, start=B4=5 and step=1 (fn_sequence, evaluator.rs:10156-10190), producing a 6x20 block of 120 cells running 5..124 whose anchor is 5, not 20 -- wrong value AND wrong shape. Six values. Every one is a small integer, exactly representable in binary floating point, and 5 is exact too, so no rounding decision exists. Spill = 6 rows x 1 column, anchor D2 = 20. tasks.intent: In E2, use one formula to list the ticket IDs from A2:A7 that are both High priority (column B) and Open (column C). If no ticket matches both conditions, the formula must return the text None instead of an error.

distractor.why: The conditions are right but the if_empty argument is missing, so with zero matching rows fn_sequence's sibling fn_filter falls past the args.len() >= 3 test and returns CellError::Value -- a literal #VALUE! error (evaluator.rs:9756-9762) -- instead of the text "None" the intent requires. A second trap fails from the other side: the one-condition version =FILTER(A2:A7,B2:B7="High","None") finds two High rows and spills {"T-102";"T-105"}, so it never reaches the fallback at all and its anchor reads "T-102".

tasks.handCheck: Evaluate (Priority="High") * (Status="Open") for rows 2-7. T-101: Low=0, Open=1 -> 0. T-102: High=1, Closed=0 -> 0. T-103: Low=0, Closed=0 -> 0. T-104: Medium=0, Open=1 -> 0. tasks.intent: In D2, work out the average of the five order amounts in B2:B6 (the Total row in row 7 is not an order and must be left out), then round that average to the NEAREST multiple of 5 — nearest in either direction, not always upward.

distractor.why: CEILING(number, significance) rounds UP to a multiple of 5 rather than to the nearest one. The average is 1221.4, which is nearer 1220 than 1225, so CEILING returns 1225 instead of 1220. Two further traps the fixture now catches: =ROUND(AVERAGE(B2:B6),0) rounds to the nearest whole number and returns 1221; =MROUND(AVERAGE(B2:B7),5) swallows the Total row (12214/6 = 2035.667) and returns 2035.

tasks.handCheck: B2:B6 = 1240 + 985 + 1310 + 1122 + 1450. 1240+985=2225; +1310=3535; +1122=4657; +1450=6107. AVERAGE = 6107/5 = 1221.4. fn_mround (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:16345) computes (number/multiple).round()*multiple = (1221.4/5).round()*5 = (244.28).round()*5 = 244*5 = 1220, an exact integer in binary floating point. tasks.intent: In D2, report the median number of resolution hours across the tickets in B2:B8 — the middle value, and with an even count of numbers the average of the two middle values. Ticket T-06 is still open and has no hours logged, so its empty cell is not part of the population and must not be counted as a zero.

A second failure mode the fixture catches: treating the empty B7 as a zero gives the sorted list 0,2,3,4,6,9,71 — an odd count of seven — with a median of 4.

tasks.handCheck: B7 is never written, so it is absent from the grid. eval_range (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:1841) materialises absent cells in a rectangle as Blank, NOT Number(0.0) — its own comment calls the zero-injection 'THE REAL DEFECT' — and collect_numbers_recursive (evaluator.rs:4132) has the arm `EvalResult::Blank => {}` at line 4140, so the blank is dropped rather than collected. tasks.intent: In E2, find the variable cost per unit: the slope of the least-squares straight line that predicts Cost (column C) from Units (column B) across the six production batches in rows 2 to 7. The batches do not lie exactly on a straight line, so use all six of them in a least-squares fit rather than any two of them. Cost is the value being predicted and Units is the predictor. The Total row in row 8 is not a batch and must be left out.

distractor.why: SLOPE takes known_y first and known_x second (SLOPE(known_y, known_x)); writing the x range first regresses Units on Cost and returns 150000/3752750 = 0.03997068816, not 25. Two further traps the fixture now catches: the two-point shortcut =(C7-C2)/(B7-B2) reads 2240/90 = 24.888..., and =SLOPE(C2:C8,B2:B8) pulls in the Total row pair (300 units, 9390 cost) and returns 30.6654676.

tasks.handCheck: fn_slope (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:12623) pairs the two ranges, then returns sum((x-mean_x)*(y-mean_y)) / sum((x-mean_x)^2). x = 10,20,40,50,80,100, sum 300, mean_x = 50 exactly. y = 600,800,1300,1550,2300,2840, sum 9390, mean_y = 1565 exactly. dx = -40,-30,-10,0,30,50. dy = -965,-765,-265,-15,735,1275. Products dx*dy = 38600, 22950, 2650, 0, 22050, 63750; sum_xy = 38600+22950=61550; +2650=64200; +22050=86250; +63750=150000. sum_x2 = 1600+900+100+0+900+2500 = 6000. slope = 150000/6000 = 25 exactly — both means are integers and every intermediate is an integer, so nothing rounds in f64. (The line is Cost = 25*Units + 315, and only four of the six batches sit on it: B-01 is 285 above it and B-06 is 25 below it, so no pair of endpoints reproduces the fit.)

tasks.intent: In D2, calculate the fixed monthly payment on the loan described in B1:B4: the loan amount is in B1, the annual interest rate in B2, the term in years in B3 and the number of payments per year in B4. Use the monthly rate (annual rate divided by payments per year) and the total number of payments (years times payments per year). Payments are made at the END of each month, and nothing is left owing at the end of the term. The arrangement fee in B5 is paid up front in cash and is not financed, so it is not part of the loan amount. Keep PMT's own sign — the answer is a negative number — and round it to 2 decimals.

distractor.why: It feeds the ANNUAL rate 0.06 into a formula that still counts 60 monthly periods, so it charges 6% per month. PMT(0.06,60,240000) = -14850.17, more than three times the true payment of -4639.87. Two further traps the fixture catches: folding the 2500 arrangement fee into the principal as B1+B5 finances money that is actually paid in cash and gives -4688.20; and paying at the start of each month, =ROUND(PMT(B2/B4,B3*B4,B1,0,1),2), gives -4616.79.

tasks.handCheck: rate = 0.06/12 = 0.005 exactly; nper = 5*12 = 60; pv = 240000; fv = 0 (omitted); type = 0 (omitted, i.e. end of period). fn_pmt (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:8945) takes the args in the order rate, nper, pv, [fv], [type], computes pvif = (1+rate)^nper = 1.005^60 = 1.3488501525493075, then pmt = rate*(pv*pvif + fv)/(pvif - 1) = 0.005*240000*1.3488501525493075/0.3488501525493075 = 1618.6201830591690/0.3488501525493075 = 4639.872367062785, and returns -pmt because type != 1. So PMT = -4639.872367062785 (recomputed independently in IEEE-754 double arithmetic, not taken from the author). fn_round (evaluator.rs:4899) computes (num * 10^digits).round() / 10^digits = (-463987.2367062785).round()/100 = -463987/100 = -4639.87. Not a halfway case, so the round-half-away-from-zero convention does not bite.

tasks.intent: In D2, calculate the net present value of the project in A1:B7 using a discount rate of 10% per year, rounded to 2 decimals. The Year 0 outlay in B2 happens today, so it is already at present value and must NOT be discounted; only the Year 1 to Year 5 cash flows in B3:B7 get discounted, the first of them by one year.

distractor.why: NPV discounts its FIRST value by one full period, so putting the Year 0 outlay inside the range treats -50000 as if it were spent at the end of Year 1 and pushes all five later flows one year further out as well. It returns 12863.63 instead of 14149.99 — an error of 1286.36 that still looks like a plausible NPV, which is why this mistake survives review. A second trap: subtracting the outlay, =ROUND(NPV(0.1,B3:B7)-B2,2), double-counts its sign and returns 64149.99.

Running total in double arithmetic = 64149.98975479816. Adding the undiscounted B2 = -50000 gives 14149.98975479816. fn_round (evaluator.rs:4899) computes (14149.98975479816 * 100).round()/100 = (1414998.975479816).round()/100 = 1414999/100 = 14149.99. Recomputed independently, not read off the author's figures.

tasks.intent: In the supplier quote table in A1:C9, find the LOWEST single Price among the rows where the Material is Steel AND the Certified column says Yes. Cheaper quotes that are for a different material, or that are not certified, must be ignored even though they are lower. Put the result in E2.

distractor.why: Dropping the Certified condition keeps every Steel row, so the uncertified Steel quote of 210 (row 3) is now the cheapest and wins. It computes 210 instead of 390 — and 210 is a quote the buyer may not legally accept, which is why the second condition is the whole point of the request.

tasks.handCheck: Eight data rows, tested against Material=Steel AND Certified=Yes. r2 Steel/Yes 480 IN. r3 Steel/No 210 OUT (not certified). r4 Copper/Yes 150 OUT (wrong material). r5 Steel/Yes 390 IN. r6 Copper/No 900 OUT (both). r7 Steel/Yes 640 IN. r8 Copper/Yes 270 OUT (wrong material). r9 Steel/No 330 OUT (not certified). min(480, 390, 640) = 390. Every near-miss reading is deliberately LOWER, so it cannot coincide: MIN over the whole Price column is 150, MINIFS on Material=Steel alone is 210, MINIFS on Certified=Yes alone is 150. All four prices are integers below 2^53, exact in binary64, and there are no ties.

tasks.intent: The table in A1:B9 lists orders with a Date and an Amount. Cell E1 holds the first day of the reporting window and cell E2 holds the last day. Add up the Amount for every order whose Date falls inside that window INCLUSIVELY — an order dated exactly on the day in E1 counts, and so does one dated exactly on the day in E2. Build the criteria from E1 and E2 rather than typing the dates into the formula. Put the total in E4.

distractor.why: Strict inequalities exclude the two orders that sit exactly ON the window boundaries: the 1200 dated 2025-01-01 and the 900 dated 2025-03-31. It computes 100+600+300 = 1000 instead of 3100, so two thirds of the quarter's revenue silently disappears from the report.

tasks.handCheck: Typing 2025-01-01 into a cell stores a DATE, not text: the engine reports ISNUMBER(E1) = TRUE and E1+0 = 45658, so the comparison is numeric on date serials. E1 = 45658 (2025-01-01), E2 = 45747 (2025-03-31). Row by row against 45658 <= date <= 45747: r2 2024-12-31 = 45657, below the start, OUT. r3 2025-01-01 = 45658, EQUAL to the start so the >= keeps it, IN 1200. r4 2025-01-20 IN 100. r5 2025-02-28 IN 600. r6 2025-03-31 = 45747, EQUAL to the end so the <= keeps it, IN 900. r7 2025-04-01 = 45748, one day past the end, OUT. r8 2025-06-15 OUT. r9 2025-02-14 IN 300. 1200 + 100 + 600 + 900 + 300 = 3100. The two just-outside rows are deliberately the largest in the table (4000 and 8000), so an off-by-one that admits either is enormous rather than subtle: the whole column sums to 15600. Concatenating the operator onto the cell is also the only form this engine accepts — a criteria string carrying a date LITERAL, such as ">=2025-01-01", is never coerced to a date here and silently matches nothing (measured: 0). That is a Calcula deviation from Excel, filed in engineFindings; the task is written against cell-held bounds so it measures the model rather than that defect.

tasks.intent: The stock table in A1:C9 has an Item, a Quantity and a Value. Cell E1 holds a minimum quantity, which the user will change from time to time. Add up the VALUE of every item whose QUANTITY is greater than or equal to whatever number is in E1 — read the threshold from E1, do not type a number into the formula. Note that the column being tested and the column being added are different. Put the total in E3.

distractor.why: The sum range and the criteria range have traded places. This is the argument-order trap: SUMIF takes (range, criteria, sum_range) and puts the TESTED column first, while SUMIFS takes (sum_range, criteria_range, criteria) and puts the ADDED column first, so a model that keeps SUMIF's habit while switching function names tests Value and adds Quantity. Every Value is at least 150, so the >=50 test passes on all eight rows and it adds the whole Quantity column, 120+30+50+45+200+10+75+20 = 550, instead of 2750 — a count of parts reported as money.

Near-miss readings are all far away, and all four were measured against this fixture rather than reasoned about: strict ">" drops Washers and gives 2600; summing Quantity instead of Value gives 445; applying the threshold to the Value column admits every row and gives the whole Value column, 840+210+150+990+1300+2400+460+180 = 6530; and swapping which column is tested and which is added — SUMIF's argument order kept under SUMIFS, which is the distractor — gives the whole Quantity column, 550. None of the five values collide. The threshold is NOT stated in the intent, only its location, so a model that hardcodes a literal has to read it off the sheet; note that the grader compares VALUES, so a hardcoded ">=50" still scores correct here — the cell reference is asked for because it is the robust form, not because this task can measure it.

tasks.intent: In the order table in A1:C9, add up the Amount for every order in the West region whose Status is anything OTHER than Cancelled. Shipped, Pending and Delivered orders all count; only Cancelled ones are left out, and orders outside the West region are left out whatever their status. Put the total in E2.

distractor.why: Losing the <> inverts the condition: instead of everything except Cancelled it keeps ONLY the Cancelled West orders, 9000 and 7000. It computes 16000 instead of 1250 — it reports the money that was thrown away as though it were the money that was earned.

tasks.handCheck: The exclusion has to be written as a criterion rather than by listing the wanted statuses, because the request says 'anything other than Cancelled' and the table carries three different keeper statuses. Eight data rows against Region=West AND Status<>Cancelled. r2 West/Shipped IN 400. r3 West/Cancelled OUT 9000. r4 East/Shipped OUT (region). r5 West/Pending IN 600. r6 West/Cancelled OUT 7000. r7 East/Cancelled OUT (both). r8 West/Delivered IN 250. r9 East/Pending OUT (region). 400 + 600 + 250 = 1250. The two cancelled West orders are deliberately by far the biggest numbers in the table, so every wrong reading overshoots enormously and cannot coincide: West with no status test at all is 400+9000+600+7000+250 = 17250; the inverted reading is 16000; not-Cancelled with no region test is 400+5000+600+250+1200 = 7450. All integers, exact in binary64.

tasks.intent: In the report table in A1:C9, add up the Amount for the rows whose Code is one of the 2025 quarterly codes AND whose Status is Final. A quarterly code is the letter Q, then EXACTLY ONE character, then -2025 — so Q1-2025 through Q4-2025 qualify, but the month code Q12-2025 has two characters after the Q and must not be included, and neither must a code with anything appended after the year, such as Q3-2025-REV. Put the total in E2.

distractor.why: The * wildcard stands for any run of characters, including two, so it also matches the monthly code Q12-2025 and pulls in its 5000. It computes 120+340+5000+410+1500 = 7370 instead of 2370 — a month double-counted into a quarterly total, which is exactly the error the single-character ? is there to prevent.

tasks.handCheck: Calcula anchors a wildcard pattern to the WHOLE cell text, so "Q?-2025" means the code is exactly seven characters: Q, any one character, then -2025. Verified against the engine: over a fixture of AB1/AXB/AXXB/XB, SUMIF with "A?B" matched only AXB while "A*B" matched AXB and AXXB. Row by row against Code matches Q?-2025 AND Status=Final: r2 Q1-2025/Final IN 120. r3 Q2-2025/Final IN 340. r4 Q12-2025: the ? consumes the 1, then the pattern needs '-' where the text has '2' — no match, OUT 5000. r5 Q3-2025 matches the code but its Status is Draft, OUT 260. r6 Q1-2024: the pattern needs -2025 and the text ends -2024, OUT 880. r7 Q4-2025/Final IN 410. r8 Q3-2025-REV: the pattern is exhausted after -2025 but four characters of text remain, and because the match is anchored to the whole cell it fails, OUT 7000. r9 Q3-2025/Final IN 1500. 120 + 340 + 410 + 1500 = 2370. The three code-shaped rejects carry the three largest amounts (5000, 7000, 880) and the status-reject carries 260, so no wrong reading lands on 2370: widening ? to * gives 7370, dropping the Status test gives 2630, and an unanchored 'contains' reading would add the 7000.

tasks.intent: The ticket log in A1:B10 has a Priority and a Team. Count how many tickets are BOTH Critical priority AND owned by the Billing team. Both conditions have to hold on the same row: a Critical ticket belonging to some other team does not count, and neither does a Billing ticket at a lower priority. Whatever the tally comes to, the cell must end up holding a NUMBER — never an error and never a blank. Put the count in D2.

distractor.why: COUNTIF takes exactly one range and one criterion, so reaching for it means the Team condition is never applied at all. It counts all three Critical tickets, every one of which belongs to Platform or Search, and computes 3 instead of 0 — it reports a Billing escalation that does not exist.

tasks.handCheck: Nine data rows. Critical rows: r2 Platform, r4 Platform, r7 Search — three of them, none Billing. Billing rows: r3 High, r5 Low, r8 High, r10 Medium — four of them, none Critical. The intersection is therefore empty and the count is 0. The intent deliberately does NOT say that the answer is zero — an earlier draft said 'the cell must show the number 0', which would have let a model score by typing =0 without doing the task at all; it now only rules out an error or a blank, which is the property being tested. This is the point of the task: an empty match set is a legitimate answer of 0, not an error, and the engine agrees — measured directly, COUNTIFS over a criterion matching nothing returns the number 0, as does SUMIFS, while AVERAGEIFS over an empty match set returns #DIV/0! because it would have to divide by zero. The two single-condition readings are both non-zero and differ from each other as well as from 0: COUNTIF on Priority alone is 3, COUNTIF on Team alone is 4, and COUNTA over the whole Priority range is 9, so nothing plausible coincides with the right answer.

tasks.intent: The ledger in A1:B9 has a Region and an Amount, where a refund is recorded as a NEGATIVE Amount. Add up the gross sales for the North region: that is, the Amount of the North rows that are greater than zero, with the North refunds left out of the total entirely rather than subtracted from it. Put the result in D2.

distractor.why: With only the region test, the North refunds are still in the range and, being negative, they are NETTED against the sales rather than excluded. It computes 1200-450+800-900+250 = 900 instead of 2250 — the answer to 'net revenue', which is a different question from the gross sales that were asked for.

tasks.handCheck: The second criterion has to be applied to the SAME column that is being added, which is the wrinkle here: the amount column is both the sum range and a criteria range. Eight data rows against Region=North AND Amount>0. r2 North 1200 IN. r3 North -450 is a refund, fails >0, OUT. r4 South 3000 OUT (region). r5 North 800 IN. r6 South -2000 OUT (both). r7 North -900 refund, OUT. r8 North 250 IN. r9 East 1500 OUT (region). 1200 + 800 + 250 = 2250. Excluding versus netting is what separates the answers, and the refunds are large enough that the two cannot coincide: netting gives 900, a 1350 gap. Other near misses also miss — all positive amounts regardless of region is 1200+3000+800+250+1500 = 6750, and the whole column is 3400. All values are integers, exact in binary64, and the sign convention is stated in the intent so 'greater than zero' is unambiguous.

tasks.intent: A2:A6 holds product names and row 1 holds the field headings: B1 Supplier, C1 Lead time, D1 Unit cost, E1 Stock, with the values in B2:E6. Two cells say what to fetch: G1 holds the product name and G2 holds the name of the field. In cell I2, return the value from the row named in G1 and the column whose heading matches G2, reading BOTH the product and the field name from those cells rather than typing either into the formula, so that changing G1 or G2 changes the answer. The column position must be found from the heading, not hard-coded, because the field columns may later be reordered.

distractor.why: The two coordinate systems disagree by one column. INDEX is given the value block B2:E6, whose first column is B, but the heading MATCH is given A1:E1, whose first column is A. MATCH("Unit cost",A1:E1,0) counts Product, Supplier, Lead time, Unit cost and answers 4, while INDEX needs 3 to reach column D. INDEX(B2:E6,3,4) therefore lands one column to the RIGHT, on E4 = 6 (the Stock figure) instead of D4 = 410 (the Unit cost). This is the classic column-index-counted-from-the-wrong-origin error in its INDEX+MATCH form, and it is silent: 6 is a perfectly plausible number for this table and no error appears anywhere. Hard-coding is the other half of the same confusion: =VLOOKUP(G1,A2:E6,3,FALSE) counts from the left edge of A2:E6 and answers 35, the Lead time, and it cannot follow G2 at all.

tasks.handCheck: MATCH(G1,A2:A6,0): G1 is the text "Pergola"; A2:A6 is Trellis, Awning, Pergola, Gazebo, Canopy, so fn_match's match_type-0 branch (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:8519-8538) returns i+1 at the first exact_lookup_equal hit, i.e. 3. MATCH(G2,B1:E1,0): G2 is the text "Unit cost"; B1:E1 is Supplier, Lead time, Unit cost, Stock, so it returns 3. INDEX(B2:E6,3,3): B2:E6 is a literal same-sheet rect, so fn_index takes the fast path (evaluator.rs:8401-8430) with rows=5, cols=4; args.len()==3 so one_index is false and cols>1, giving flat_idx = row_num*cols + col_num = 2*4 + 2 = 10 after both arguments are decremented by one at lines 8403 and 8409. 10 < rows*cols = 20, so no #REF!. r = row(B2) + 10/4 = row 2 + 2 = row 4, and c = col(B) + 10%4 = col B + 2 = col D. The cell is D4 = 410, an integer and therefore exact in binary floating point. Excluded and why: C4 = 35 is Pergola's Lead time (one column left), E4 = 6 is Pergola's Stock (one column right, and exactly what the named distractor returns), and D5 = 690 is Gazebo's Unit cost (one row down).

tasks.intent: This sheet is laid out sideways: the month headings Jan to Jun run across row 1 in B1:G1, and each metric occupies one row underneath, labelled in column A - Units in row 2, Revenue in row 3, Returns in row 4. In cell B6, return the Revenue figure for the month Apr, matching the month heading exactly across row 1 so the formula still finds the right column if the months are reordered. Revenue, not Units.

distractor.why: row_index_num counts rows from the TOP OF table_array, and the top of B1:G4 is the month heading row. Revenue is therefore row 3 of the table even though it is only the second row of data. Counting the data rows instead gives 2, and fn_hlookup returns rows[2-1][3] = E2 = 140 - April's Units - rather than rows[3-1][3] = E3 = 8750. Nothing errors: the formula hands back a number off the wrong metric row, which is the horizontal twin of the VLOOKUP col_index_num-from-the-wrong-origin bug. The other reflex is to reach for VLOOKUP on a sideways table; =VLOOKUP("Apr",B1:G4,3,FALSE) searches the first COLUMN (Jan, 120, 7500, 4) for "Apr", finds nothing and returns #N/A.

tasks.handCheck: B1:G4 is a literal same-sheet rect with rows=4 > 1 and cols=6 > 1, so fn_hlookup (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:16067-16166) is eligible for the cached path and otherwise scans; both spellings address identically. range_lookup is the literal FALSE, so args.len() > 3 takes the EvalResult::Boolean(false) arm at line 16099 and the exact branch at line 16151 runs. The first row of the table is B1:G1 = Jan, Feb, Mar, Apr, May, Jun. "Apr" carries no wildcard, so wildcard_pattern is None and the loop tests exact_lookup_equal, which hits at j = 3 (zero-based). The function returns rows[row_index - 1].get(j) = rows[2][3], and rows[2] is the THIRD row of B1:G4, i.e. sheet row 3 (Revenue). Column offset 3 from B is column E. The cell is E3 = 8750, an integer and exact in binary floating point. Excluded and why: E2 = 140 is April's Units (row index 2, what the distractor returns), E4 = 9 is April's Returns (row index 4), D3 = 8000 is March's Revenue and F3 = 9430 is May's, so no neighbouring cell in either direction shares the value 8750.
