tasks.handCheck: B2:B8 = 34, 12, 51, 19, 27, 8, 43 - seven distinct integers, so the ordering is total and no tie rule is involved. Sorted ascending: 8 (Falcon, row 7), 12 (Beacon, row 3), 19 (Delta, row 5), 27 (Ember, row 6), 34 (Aurora, row 2), 43 (Granite, row 8), 51 (Cedar, row 4). The 2nd entry is 12, so SMALL(B2:B8,2) = 12. Rows the answer must exclude: row 7 (8 hours) is SMALLER and is the one a MIN answer would return; rows 5, 6, 2, 8 and 4 are all larger. Every value is a small integer, exact in binary floating point, so no rounding decision enters. Distractor check: sorted descending the list is 51, 43, 34, 27, 19, 12, 8, so LARGE(B2:B8,2) = 43, which is 31 away from 12 and cannot coincide. The header row 1 holds the text 'Hours' and is outside B2:B8; had it been included, SMALL would still have skipped the text, so the exclusion is not load-bearing here and the intent does not lean on it.

tasks.intent: The table in A1:B9 lists eight drivers and each one's best lap time in whole seconds; a LOWER time is a better result. In D8, return Gustav's position in the standings - that is, the rank of his lap time in B8 among all eight times in B2:B9, with the FASTEST (lowest) time counting as position 1 and the slowest as position 8. All eight times are different, so there are no ties to break.

distractor.why: Order 0 - and an OMITTED third argument, which defaults to 0 - is DESCENDING ranking, where the largest number is rank 1. On lap times the largest number is the slowest driver, so it answers 7 (only David's 86 is faster, but six drivers are slower and all six are counted ahead of Gustav) instead of 2. This is the inverted-order confusion: the corpus already has rank-row-position-with-ties, where descending is correct and passing 1 is the mistake, so this task is the mirror and a model that has simply memorised 'RANK takes 0' fails one of the pair. The fixture puts Gustav second from the fast end, so the two readings are five positions apart.

tasks.handCheck: B2:B9 = 92, 88, 96, 86, 91, 99, 87, 94 - eight distinct integers. Sorted ascending: 86 (David), 87 (Gustav), 88 (Bertil), 91 (Erik), 92 (Alma), 94 (Hanna), 96 (Cecilia), 99 (Frida). The target value is B8 = 87, the 2nd entry, so the ascending rank is 2. Derived the way the engine computes it (fn_rank, core/engine/src/evaluator.rs): with a non-zero order it counts values strictly LESS than the number and adds 1 - strictly less than 87 is 86 alone, so 1 + 1 = 2. Ties are impossible here, so RANK.EQ and RANK.AVG agree and a model that reaches for either gets 2; only the DIRECTION is under test. Distractor check: descending counts values strictly GREATER than 87, which is 92, 88, 96, 91, 99 and 94 = 6 values, so 6 + 1 = 7. 2 versus 7 on an eight-row table, five positions apart, so no rounding or off-by-one reading can bridge them. Cross-check of the whole ascending column, to prove no other value is 2: David 1, Gustav 2, Bertil 3, Erik 4, Alma 5, Hanna 6, Cecilia 7, Frida 8 - exactly one driver holds position 2 and it is the one the intent names.

tasks.intent: The table in A1:C9 lists eight sales reps with their region and their revenue for the year. In E2, return the NAME of the rep with the highest revenue - the text from column A on the row that holds the largest number in C2:C9, not the revenue figure itself. All eight revenue figures are different, so exactly one rep is top.

distractor.why: This finds the right ROW and then reports the wrong COLUMN: it returns the winning revenue, the number 9400, where the task asks for the name 'Erik'. Ranking a column and then forgetting to travel back to the label is the single most common failure in this family - the model solves the hard half (locating the maximum) and skips the easy half (looking up beside it). The gap is not a near miss but a category error, a number where text was wanted, so it can never be graded as correct by accident on any fixture.

tasks.handCheck: C2:C9 = 5200, 8900, 4100, 7600, 9400, 3300, 6700, 8100 - eight distinct integers. Sorted descending: 9400, 8900, 8100, 7600, 6700, 5200, 4100, 3300. The maximum is 9400, which sits in C6. MATCH(9400, C2:C9, 0) counts positions from the START OF THE RANGE, not from row 1: C2 is position 1, C3 is 2, C4 is 3, C5 is 4, C6 is 5 - so MATCH returns 5. INDEX(A2:A9, 5) takes the 5th cell of A2:A9, which is A6 = 'Erik'. Cross-check that no accidental reading also produces 'Erik': the first data row holds Alma, the last holds Hanna, alphabetically first is Alma and alphabetically last is Hanna, and the row with the LOWEST revenue (3300) is Frida - Erik is reachable only by actually ranking column C, which is the point of the task. The two ranges A2:A9 and C2:C9 are the same height (8 cells), so INDEX and MATCH stay aligned and the header row, which holds the TEXT 'Revenue' and would be a position-0 offset error if included, is outside both. Distractor check: MAX(C2:C9) = 9400, a number, against an expectation of the text 'Erik' - different kind, different value, no coincidence possible.

tasks.intent: The table in A1:C9 lists eight sales reps with their region and the amount each one sold. In E2, return the SECOND highest amount among the North rows only - look only at the rows whose region in B2:B9 is North, and return the second largest of those amounts. The four North amounts are all different, so there is no tie. Rows in other regions must be ignored even when their amounts are larger.

distractor.why: MAXIFS gets the SUBSET right and the POSITION wrong: it can only ever return the single highest value in the region, 7800 (Cecilia), where the task asks for the one below it, 5400 (Gustav). There is no 'second' argument to MAXIFS, so reaching for it is a dead end no matter how the criteria are written - the request has to be re-expressed as LARGE over a filtered array (or an equivalent, such as LARGE of an IF-masked range). This is the 'MAX where LARGE(...,n) was needed on a filtered subset' confusion, and it is the complement of the existing rank-highest-amount-in-region, whose distractor drops the condition instead of the position, so the two tasks separate the two halves of the same request.

tasks.handCheck: North rows are 2 (4200), 4 (7800), 6 (3500) and 8 (5400) - four rows, four distinct amounts. Sorted descending within North: 7800, 5400, 4200, 3500. The 2nd entry is 5400, so the answer is 5400 (Gustav, row 8). Non-North rows and why each must be excluded: row 3 South 9100 and row 5 South 8600 are both LARGER than every North amount, and row 9 South 7200 and row 7 Central 6900 sit between the North first and second places - so a formula that ignores the region cannot land on 5400 from any position. Concretely: LARGE(C2:C9,2) over the whole column, sorted descending 9100, 8600, 7800, 7200, 6900, 5400, 4200, 3500, gives 8600; MAX(C2:C9) gives 9100; and 5400 is only the SIXTH largest overall, so the region condition is genuinely load-bearing. FILTER(C2:C9, B2:B9="North") is the idiomatic subset here because the comparison operator lifts over the range to give TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE and FILTER keeps the four TRUE positions in order. All amounts are integers, exact in binary floating point. Distractor check: MAXIFS(C2:C9,B2:B9,"North") = 7800, which is 2400 away from 5400 and is itself a North amount, so the two cannot coincide.

tasks.intent: The table in A1:B8 lists seven months and the units sold in each. In D2, return the POSITION of the busiest month within the list - a whole number between 1 and 7, where the first data row (January, row 2) is position 1 and the last (July, row 8) is position 7. Return that position number, not the month's name, not its sheet row number and not the units figure. All seven unit counts are different, so exactly one month is the busiest.

distractor.why: The positional machinery is right and the DIRECTION is inverted: this locates the quietest month instead of the busiest, returning 2 (February, 95 units) rather than 6 (June, 480 units). It is the LARGE/SMALL swap in its MAX/MIN spelling, and it is the mistake that survives review because the formula looks structurally correct - MATCH over the same range with the same exact-match flag - and only the inner aggregate is wrong. The fixture deliberately puts the minimum near the start and the maximum near the end, four positions apart, so the two answers cannot be confused for one another or for an off-by-one.

tasks.handCheck: B2:B8 = 140, 95, 310, 260, 175, 480, 220 - seven distinct integers. MAX = 480. Walking the range from its first cell: B2 is position 1 (140), B3 is 2 (95), B4 is 3 (310), B5 is 4 (260), B6 is 5 (175), B7 is 6 (480) - so MATCH(480, B2:B8, 0) = 6, and June is the 6th month listed. The exact-match flag 0 matters and the fixture is unsorted on purpose: 140, 95, 310, ... is neither ascending nor descending, so an approximate match has no defined meaning over it. Two adjacent wrong answers the intent rules out explicitly: 480 is the UNITS figure (what MAX alone returns) and 7 is the SHEET ROW of June (what ROW() or a MATCH over B1:B8 would return, since including the header text 'Units' shifts every position by one). Distractor check: MIN = 95, which sits in B3 = position 2, so the distractor returns 2, four positions away from 6. Cross-check that no other month is 6th: the seven positions map one-to-one onto the seven months, and position 6 is June alone. All counts are integers, exact in binary floating point.

tasks.intent: The table in A1:C9 lists eight reps with their region and sales. Column D should show each rep's rank WITHIN THEIR OWN REGION - highest sales in that region is 1, second highest in that region is 2, and so on - so the North reps are ranked 1 to 4 among themselves and the South reps 1 to 4 among themselves. Write the formula for cell D8, Gustav's row, who is in North. It is meant to be filled down the whole of D2:D9, so it must read both the region and the sales figure from its own row rather than typing North or Gustav's figure into the formula, and the two table ranges it scans must stay pinned to rows 2 through 9 as it is copied.

distractor.why: This is the whole-table rank, and it is what a model writes when it hears 'rank' and stops reading before 'within their own region'. RANK.EQ has no criteria argument at all, so the region can only enter by counting - the request has to be re-expressed as a conditional count of the rows that beat this one. On this fixture it answers 6, because the FOUR South reps who out-sell Gustav - 9100, 8200, 7000 and 6400 - are counted against him on top of the one row that genuinely should be, Cecilia's 5600. It is also visibly wrong as a filled-down column: it would number the eight reps 1 to 8 overall, so the North block would read 5, 6, 7, 8 and Cecilia - top of her own region - would come out 5 rather than 1. One caution for anyone re-targeting this task: on this fixture the four South reps happen to hold the top four places overall, so on rows 3, 5, 7 and 9 the region-blind rank coincides with the within-region rank. The target row must therefore stay in North, which rows 2, 4, 6 and 8 are; D8 is one of them.

tasks.handCheck: The target row is 8: Gustav, North, 5100. North rows are 2 (Alma 4200), 4 (Cecilia 5600), 6 (Erik 3500) and 8 (Gustav 5100). Sorted descending within North: 5600, 5100, 4200, 3500 - Gustav is 2nd, so the answer is 2. Derived the way the formula computes it: COUNTIFS applies both criteria row by row and counts rows where region equals B8's value ('North') AND sales are strictly greater than C8's value (5100). Row 2: North but 4200 is not > 5100, no. Row 4: North and 5600 > 5100, YES. Row 6: North but 3500 is not > 5100, no. Row 8: North but 5100 is not strictly greater than itself, no - which is exactly why the count is of rows that BEAT this one and the +1 converts 'how many are ahead' into 'what place is this'. Rows 3, 5, 7 and 9 are South and fail the first criterion regardless of their amounts. Count = 1, so 1 + 1 = 2. The '>' is glued to the cell with & because a criteria string must be built as text; a bare >C8 would be read as a literal. Excluded and why it matters: the FOUR South figures above Gustav's - 9100, 8200, 7000 and 6400 - are precisely what the whole-table reading adds to Cecilia's 5600. Cross-check of the overall descending order, 9100, 8200, 7000, 6400, 5600, 5100, 4200, 3500, puts 5100 at position 6, so the region-blind answer is 6 = 5 rows ahead + 1, and the two readings are four places apart. That gap exists only on the NORTH rows: the four South figures are the four largest in the table, so a region-blind rank on rows 3, 5, 7 and 9 returns 1, 4, 2 and 3 - the same numbers the within-region formula returns there. The target must stay on a North row (2, 4, 6 or 8) for the task to separate the two readings at all, and D8 is Gustav's, in North. Cross-check that the intent's claim about the whole column holds - that each region really is numbered 1 to 4 - the same formula on the other rows gives Cecilia 1, Gustav 2, Alma 3, Erik 4 for North and Bertil 1, Frida 2, Hanna 3, David 4 for South, so each region's four ranks are a permutation of 1 to 4 with no gaps and no repeats. The pinning is load-bearing for the fill-down even though the target row alone cannot show it: with $B$2:$B$9 and $C$2:$C$9 fixed and B8/C8 relative, copying into D2 scans the same eight rows against Alma's own region and figure; without the pins the scanned window would slide off the table. All figures are integers, exact in binary floating point.

tasks.intent: The table in A1:B10 lists nine students and their quiz points. In D5, return David's rank among all nine point totals in B2:B10, with the HIGHEST score counting as rank 1. Four students are tied on 80 points, and the tie must be resolved the AVERAGED way: the four tied students share the average of the four places their block occupies, rather than all four taking the best place in the block. The answer is therefore allowed to be a fraction.

distractor.why: RANK.EQ is COMPETITION ranking: every member of a tied block takes the BEST place in the block, so all four 80s would be rank 3 and the next distinct score would be rank 7. It answers 3 where the averaged rule gives 4.5. The two functions differ ONLY when there is a tie, which is why the fixture carries a four-way one and why the intent spells out which convention is wanted - the distinction is invisible on distinct data and a model that treats the two names as synonyms passes every tie-free task in the corpus. RANK.EQ is also what a bare RANK resolves to, so the wrong answer is the one reached by writing the most familiar name.

tasks.handCheck: B2:B10 = 95, 80, 91, 80, 80, 80, 72, 65, 60 - nine values, four of them tied at 80 (Bertil, David, Erik, Frida). Sorted descending: 95, 91, 80, 80, 80, 80, 72, 65, 60, so the tied block occupies places 3, 4, 5 and 6. The averaged rank is (3+4+5+6)/4 = 18/4 = 4.5. Derived the way the engine computes it: count values strictly GREATER than 80 - that is 95 and 91, so 2, giving a base place of 3 - then spread across the 4 equal values, 3 + (4-1)/2 = 3 + 1.5 = 4.5. 4.5 is exactly representable in binary floating point (9/2), so there is no tolerance question. Three rival readings, all distinct, which is why the fixture is deliberately lopsided rather than symmetric about the tie: descending competition rank is 3 (the distractor); ASCENDING averaged rank is 5.5, because sorted ascending the list is 60, 65, 72, 80, 80, 80, 80, 91, 95 and the block then occupies places 4, 5, 6, 7 for a mean of 5.5; and ascending competition rank is 4. Had the table been symmetric around the tie, the ascending and descending averaged ranks would have coincided and a model that got the direction wrong would still have scored - so the extra low score (Ivar, 60) is load-bearing and must not be trimmed. Distractor check: 3 against 4.5, a whole 1.5 apart and of different parity as a place number.

tasks.intent: The sheet Margins lists four rows in A2:C5: column B is each product's gross margin in 2024 and column C the same margin in 2025, both already stored as fractions (0.4 means a 40% margin). Row 5 is the blended all-products line. In E3, report how many PERCENTAGE POINTS the Gadget's margin moved from 2024 to 2025. Express it on the same scale as the margins themselves, so a rise of 5 percentage points is 0.05, not 5.

distractor.why: This is the percentage CHANGE in the margin, not the change in percentage points — the single most confused pair in this family. It divides by the 2024 margin, so it answers the question "the margin grew by what proportion of itself?": 0.375/0.25 = 1.5, minus 1 = 0.5. It reports 0.5 (a 50% relative improvement) where the right answer is 0.125 (a 12.5 percentage-point improvement). Both are true statements about the same pair of numbers and they differ by a factor of four here, which is exactly why a reader cannot tell which one a formula meant without looking at it.

tasks.handCheck: Gadget is row 3: B3 = 0.25 and C3 = 0.375. The change in percentage points is C3 - B3 = 0.375 - 0.25 = 0.125. Both operands are exact in binary floating point (0.375 = 3/8 = 2^-2 + 2^-3, 0.25 = 2^-2) and so is the difference (0.125 = 2^-3), so the subtraction is exact and the expectation needs no rounding. Sanity: the margin went from 25% to 37.5%, which is 12.5 percentage points, and 12.5 percentage points on this fraction scale is 0.125. No cell in the fixture holds 0.125, so the answer cannot be read off the sheet. Competing readings all land elsewhere: C3/B3 - 1 = 0.5 (the distractor), C3/B3 = 1.5, B3 - C3 = -0.125, (C3-B3)*100 = 12.5, and the all-products line C5 - B5, which the engine returns as 0.025000000000000022 rather than a clean 0.025 because 0.4 has no exact binary form — one more reason the graded row uses two exactly-representable margins.

tasks.intent: The sheet Stock lists inventory lines in A2:D7 — the warehouse in column A, the item in B, the status in C and the units in D — and row 8 is a Total row that must stay out of any denominator. In F2, compute the Oslo Bolts line (row 2) as a share of the units Oslo has IN STOCK: the denominator is the total of the Oslo lines whose status is In stock, and nothing else. Backordered lines and the Bergen warehouse are both excluded from that denominator. Give the answer as a fraction between 0 and 1, so three eighths is written 0.375, not 37.5.

distractor.why: It keeps only one of the two conditions: it subtotals Oslo but forgets the status, so the 5000 backordered Screws land in the denominator. Oslo's total becomes 3000+1000+5000+4000 = 13000 instead of 8000, and it returns 3000/13000 = 0.230769..., not 0.375. Dropping the other condition instead, =D2/SUMIF(C2:C7,"In stock",D2:D7), is wrong the mirrored way and returns 3000/17000 = 0.176470..., because it pulls Bergen's 9000 in-stock Bolts into an Oslo share. And the Total row is live bait: =D2/D8 divides by the 24000 grand total and returns 0.125.

tasks.handCheck: SUMIFS over D2:D7 keeping rows where column A is Oslo AND column C is In stock selects rows 2, 3 and 5: 3000 + 1000 + 4000 = 8000. Row 4 is Oslo but Backorder, row 6 is In stock but Bergen, row 7 is neither — all excluded. Bolts' share = D2/8000 = 3000/8000 = 3/8 = 0.375, exact in binary (0.25 + 0.125), so no rounding is needed. The ranges deliberately stop at row 7: D8 is a formula, =SUM(D2:D7) = 3000+1000+5000+4000+9000+2000 = 24000, and the Total row has no warehouse or status, so even a model that runs the criteria ranges down to row 8 gets the same 8000 — the Total row can only hurt via a SUM or a direct reference to D8. Wrong denominators and what they give: Oslo only 13000 -> 0.2308; In stock only 17000 -> 0.1765; grand total 24000 -> 0.125; Oslo In stock is the only route to 0.375.

tasks.intent: The sheet Growth has three business segments in A2:C4 with their 2024 revenue in column B and their 2025 revenue in column C; row 5 is the company total for each year. In E2, compute Retail's CONTRIBUTION TO THE COMPANY'S GROWTH: Retail's change in revenue from 2024 to 2025, divided by the company's total 2024 revenue rather than by Retail's own. Defined this way the three segments' contributions add up to the company's overall growth rate, which is the point of the measure. Give the answer as a fraction, so a contribution of 5 percentage points of growth is 0.05, not 5.

distractor.why: It divides Retail's change by RETAIL's own 2024 base instead of the company's, which is the segment's growth rate, not its contribution to the company's growth. It computes 12000/32000 = 0.375 — twice the right answer, and a number that cannot be added across segments: Retail 0.375 + Wholesale 4000/24000 = 0.1667 + Online 0 = 0.5417, which is nothing like the company's actual 25% growth. The contribution form is what sums correctly: 0.1875 + 0.0625 + 0 = 0.25.

tasks.handCheck: Retail's change = C2 - B2 = 44000 - 32000 = 12000. The company's 2024 base is B5 = SUM(B2:B4) = 32000 + 24000 + 8000 = 64000. Contribution = 12000/64000 = 3/16 = 0.1875, exact in binary (0.125 + 0.0625), so no rounding is needed. The decomposition checks out, which is the strongest proof the fixture is right: Wholesale contributes (28000-24000)/64000 = 4000/64000 = 0.0625, Online contributes (8000-8000)/64000 = 0, and 0.1875 + 0.0625 + 0 = 0.25, which equals the company's growth C5/B5 - 1 = 80000/64000 - 1 = 1.25 - 1 = 0.25. Other readings miss: Retail's own growth 12000/32000 = 0.375 (the distractor); dividing by the 2025 total 12000/80000 = 0.15; Retail's share of the growth 12000/16000 = 0.75; the shift in Retail's share of revenue C2/C5 - B2/B5 = 0.55 - 0.5, which the engine returns as 0.050000000000000044. Only the company's 2024 base gives 0.1875.

tasks.intent: The sheet Pipeline lists closed deals in A2:C7 — the rep in column A, the stage (Won or Lost) in B, and the deal's value in C. E2:E5 lists the four reps on the team, and F2:F5 is to hold each rep's win rate. Adam, in E2, joined this month and has no deals in the list at all. In F2, compute the win rate for the rep named in E2: the value of that rep's Won deals divided by the value of ALL of that rep's deals, Won and Lost together. The denominator is that rep's own total, so for a rep with no deals there is nothing to divide by, and in that case the formula must return the text No deals (exactly those characters, capital N, lower-case d) rather than an error or a zero — a zero would say the rep lost every deal, which is not what happened. Write it so it can be copied down through F5 for the other three reps: the rep name must come from column E, and the three data ranges must stay fixed on rows 2 to 7.

distractor.why: The guard is present and correct; the DENOMINATOR is wrong. It divides each rep's won value by the whole pipeline's 18000 instead of by that rep's own total, so the division can never fail and the guard can never fire. Adam's cell therefore reads 0 — the number, from 0/18000 — instead of the required text No deals, which is exactly the lie the intent forbids: it claims Adam lost every deal when he has none. It is wrong on every other row too: Ben would read 2000/18000 = 0.1111 instead of 2000/8000 = 0.25. A wrong denominator does not just change the number, it disarms the guard.

tasks.handCheck: Adam (E2) appears nowhere in A2:A7, so SUMIF($A$2:$A$7,E2,$C$2:$C$7) matches no row and returns 0. The IF test 0=0 is TRUE, so the formula takes its second argument and the cell holds the text No deals; the division in the third argument is never reached, and the result depends on no floating-point value at all. Written with IFERROR instead — =IFERROR(SUMIFS($C$2:$C$7,$A$2:$A$7,E2,$B$2:$B$7,"Won")/SUMIF($A$2:$A$7,E2,$C$2:$C$7),"No deals") — it is equally correct: the divisor is 0, so the engine's divide arm returns #DIV/0! (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:2604 tests the divisor first, whatever the numerator is, so 0/0 is #DIV/0! and not 0), and IFERROR yields the same text. Positive control that the fixture is well formed and the rest of the formula is doing real work: copied into F3, the same formula gives Ben 2000/(2000+6000) = 0.25; F4 gives Clara 1000/2000 = 0.5; F5 gives Dana 5000/8000 = 0.625. Three different rates, so the SUMIFS is not returning a constant. The distractor's denominator SUM($C$2:$C$7) = 2000+6000+1000+1000+5000+3000 = 18000, and Adam's numerator is 0, so it returns the number 0, which is not the text No deals. This is exactly the IFERROR-where-IFNA-was-required confusion, and it is a wrong ANSWER, not a parse failure - the formula evaluates cleanly to the wrong thing. The IF-shaped spelling of the same mistake, =IF(ISERROR(VLOOKUP("J-102",A2:D5,4,FALSE)),"Unknown job",VLOOKUP("J-102",A2:D5,4,FALSE)), was measured on this fixture too and also returns "Unknown job", so the task catches the confusion rather than one spelling of it.

tasks.handCheck: By hand. Row 4 of the table is the J-102 row: B4 = 450, C4 = 0, and D4 holds =B4/C4, that is 450/0, which is a division by zero and evaluates to #DIV/0!. VLOOKUP("J-102", A2:D5, 4, FALSE) is an exact-match lookup (fourth argument FALSE) down the first column of A2:D5, which holds J-100, J-101, J-102, J-103; "J-102" matches the third of those, the sheet row 4. Column 4 of the table is column D, so the lookup returns the value of D4, which is the error #DIV/0!. That error is then argument 1 of IFNA. IFNA substitutes its second argument only when argument 1 is specifically #N/A; #DIV/0! is a different error, so IFNA returns argument 1 unchanged and F2 shows #DIV/0!. Expected result: the error literal #DIV/0!. Teeth: the three healthy rows compute to distinct clean numbers - 800/20 = 40, 600/24 = 25, 900/30 = 30 - so a lookup that lands on the wrong row returns a NUMBER and can never accidentally produce an error, and a missing-code lookup would return the text, so the three outcomes (number, text, error) are mutually exclusive on this fixture. KNOWN LIMIT OF THE GRADING, recorded so the task is not over-read. Because the required answer IS an error, a formula that omits the guard ALTOGETHER also lands on #DIV/0! and scores correct: a bare =VLOOKUP("J-102",A2:D5,4,FALSE), an =INDEX(D2:D5,MATCH("J-102",A2:A5,0)), and even a bare =B4/C4 were all measured at #DIV/0! on this fixture. That cannot be designed out at single-cell granularity, because IFNA(x,fallback) is by definition identical to x for every x that is not #N/A: no one graded value can separate the correct guard from no guard AND from IFERROR at the same time. So this cell measures the over-catching half of the distinction - the half that hides a real fault behind a reassuring word - while the under-guarding half is measured by errguard-ifna-price-lookup-fallback and errguard-countif-presence-answers-no, where the fallback IS the answer and an unguarded formula returns an error instead.

tasks.intent: Cell E3 must audit the comment cell C3 and report exactly one of two words. Report the text Has content if C3 holds anything at all - and a cell holding a formula counts as holding something, even when the formula's result looks blank on screen. Report the text Empty only when the cell is genuinely empty, with nothing whatsoever in it. Spell the two answers exactly as Has content and Empty.

distractor.why: Testing a cell against an empty string instead of asking whether it is blank. The two agree on an untouched cell and disagree on exactly the cell this task is about: C3 holds a live formula, =IF(B3>=90,"Outstanding",""), and because Bruno's score is 74 that formula returns the empty text string. The comparison C3="" compares that empty string with "" and is TRUE, so the distractor answers "Empty" - the exact opposite of the required "Has content". The formula in C3 is real content: it will start printing "Outstanding" the moment the score is raised, and an audit that reports the cell as empty invites somebody to type over it and destroy it. It is not merely unlucky on this one cell either - the comparison against "" cannot distinguish 'no content' from 'content that evaluates to no text', so it answers "Empty" for every formula in the column that is currently returning the blank branch, which on a real review sheet is most of them. The length-shaped spelling of the same mistake, =IF(LEN(C3)>0,"Has content","Empty"), was measured on this fixture too and also answers "Empty" - LEN(C3) is 0 - so the task catches the confusion rather than one spelling of it.

tasks.handCheck: By hand. C3 contains the formula =IF(B3>=90,"Outstanding",""). B3 is 74, and 74 >= 90 is FALSE, so the IF takes its third argument and C3 evaluates to the empty text string "". ISBLANK asks whether the referenced CELL is empty - whether it has no content - not whether its value prints as nothing; C3 has content (a formula), so ISBLANK(C3) is FALSE. The outer IF therefore takes its third argument and E3 becomes the text "Has content", spelled with a capital H and a lowercase c as the intent requires. Expected result: the text Has content. Teeth: C4 in this fixture is genuinely empty - there is no C4 cell at all - and ISBLANK(C4) was measured TRUE, so the fixture contains both cases and the task asks about the one that separates the two readings. C2 and C5 hold ordinary text, for which both readings agree, which is why neither of them is the target. Measured on this fixture, for the record: ISBLANK(C3) FALSE, C3="" TRUE, LEN(C3) 0, COUNTA(C3) 1. The COUNTA and NOT(ISBLANK) spellings are legitimate alternatives and both return "Has content"; grading is on the value, so they are correctly scored right.

tasks.intent: Cell F4 must review the average in D4 and say whether that sensor needs attention. A sensor that is offline is deliberately marked as not available with #N/A, and that is an expected, accepted state: F4 must then show the text OK. Any OTHER error in D4 - a calculation that genuinely failed, such as a division by zero - means the sensor needs attention and F4 must show the text Check sensor. An ordinary number in D4 is fine too and also gives OK.

distractor.why: ISERROR and ISERR differ on exactly one value, #N/A, and #N/A is what D4 holds. ISERROR is TRUE for every error including #N/A, so the distractor answers "Check sensor" where "OK" is required: it raises an alarm about the one sensor whose state the operator has already recorded and accepted. It is not a near miss on this fixture - it is the wrong predicate for the question, and it would go on flagging every offline sensor in the column forever, which is how a report full of false alarms teaches its readers to ignore the real one on row 3. ISERR is the predicate that says genuine-calculation-error-but-not-not-available.

tasks.handCheck: By hand. D4 holds =NA(), the function whose entire job is to produce the value #N/A, so D4 is #N/A. ISERR is the error test that deliberately EXCLUDES #N/A: it is TRUE for #DIV/0!, #VALUE!, #REF!, #NAME?, #NUM! and #NULL!, and FALSE for #N/A and for any non-error value. D4 is #N/A, so ISERR(D4) is FALSE. The IF therefore takes its third argument and F4 becomes the text OK, in capitals as the intent requires. Expected result: the text OK. Teeth: the fixture holds all three states the intent distinguishes, and they give three different answers under the correct formula. Row 3 is a real failure - 180 total over 0 samples, so D3 is #DIV/0! - and ISERR(D3) was measured TRUE, giving "Check sensor". Rows 2 and 5 are clean numbers, 240/8 = 30 and 300/12 = 25, and ISERR of a number is FALSE, giving OK. So pointing the formula at the wrong row changes the answer on row 3, and getting the predicate wrong changes the answer on row 4. One lenience, recorded rather than hidden: =IF(ISNA(D4),"OK","Check sensor") also answers OK on this cell and so scores correct, even though it is wrong for the intent's third case - pointed at the clean number in D2 it would say Check sensor. The graded cell separates ISERR from ISERROR, which is what the task is for; it cannot additionally separate ISERR from a bare ISNA test, because those two branchings agree on every error value and differ only on an ordinary number, which is not what the graded cell holds.

tasks.intent: Cell D2 must answer one question with a word: has invoice number 4471 already been entered in the invoice-number column B2:B9? Put the text Yes in D2 if that number is somewhere in the column and the text No if it is not. D2 must always hold one of those two words - an invoice number that is absent is an ordinary, expected answer of No, and must never leave the cell showing an error of any kind.

distractor.why: Reaching for a lookup to answer a presence question. MATCH computes a POSITION, not a presence, and a position does not exist for a number that is not in the list: with 4471 absent from B2:B9, MATCH(4471,B2:B9,0) is #N/A, that error propagates straight through the comparison and out of the IF, and D2 shows #N/A instead of the word No. The requirement is explicit that absence is an ordinary answer, so the distractor fails on the only case that matters: it answers correctly for every invoice that IS in the column and breaks for every one that is not, which is precisely backwards for a duplicate check whose normal outcome is 'not a duplicate'. COUNTIF needs no guard because counting nothing is 0, not an error - that is the whole reason to prefer it here.

tasks.handCheck: By hand. The invoice-number column B2:B9 holds, in order, 4410, 4425, 4437, 4452, 4468, 4480, 4491 and 4503. 4471 is not among them: the column steps 4468 then 4480, so 4471 falls in the gap between two entries that both exist. COUNTIF(B2:B9, 4471) therefore counts zero matching cells and returns 0. The comparison 0 > 0 is FALSE, so the IF takes its third argument and D2 becomes the text No. Expected result: the text No. Teeth: 4471 sits BETWEEN two real invoice numbers rather than outside the range, so an approximate-match reading cannot fall off either end and quietly agree by accident, and no two invoice numbers in the column are equal, so the count for any number that IS present would be exactly 1 and the same formula would answer Yes. Cross-check, measured on this fixture: swapping 4471 for 4468 gives COUNTIF = 1, 1 > 0 is TRUE, and the answer flips to Yes, which confirms the comparison rather than the fixture is doing the deciding. One lenience, inherent to any question whose true answer is 'absent': a formula that searches the WRONG column, =IF(COUNTIF(A2:A9,4471)>0,"Yes","No") over the supplier names, also answers No, because 4471 is not there either. It cannot be designed out, because the distractor only bites when the key is missing - with a key that is present, MATCH would succeed and the distractor would be right. What the graded cell does separate is a counting presence test from a positional one, which is the discrimination this task is for.

tasks.intent: Cell G2 must work out the total for an order of part P-99: its unit price multiplied by the quantity in D2, then plus the shipping charge in E2. Take the unit price from the price list A2:B5 with an exact-match lookup. A part that is not in the price list is billed at the standard rate of 10 per unit, so a missing price counts as a price of 10. The shipping charge in E2 is owed on every order without exception and must be part of the total whether or not a price was found.

distractor.why: The same guard and the same fallback, wrapped around the wrong thing. Putting IFERROR around the WHOLE expression means the error from the missing lookup takes the entire arithmetic with it: the multiplication and the addition both inherit the #N/A, IFERROR catches it at the top, and the fallback replaces the TOTAL instead of replacing the PRICE. G2 becomes 10 where the correct total is 125 - and 10 is not a total at all, it is a unit rate, with the quantity of 8 and the shipping charge of 45 both silently gone, so the sheet bills an eight-unit order as if it were one unit delivered free. The intent says the shipping charge is owed on every order without exception, and this spelling is exactly how that guarantee is lost. The fallback value stands in for the price, so the guard belongs around the lookup alone; only then do the surviving terms, times 8 and plus 45, still run. 10 against 125 on the same fixture, from moving one parenthesis.

tasks.handCheck: By hand, in evaluation order. VLOOKUP("P-99", A2:B5, 2, FALSE) is an exact-match lookup down the part column, which holds P-11, P-12, P-13 and P-14. P-99 is not one of them, so the lookup finds nothing and returns #N/A. That #N/A is argument 1 of IFERROR, which catches it and yields argument 2, the number 10 - the standard rate the intent prescribes for an unlisted part. The rest of the expression then evaluates normally: 10 * D2 = 10 * 8 = 80, and 80 + E2 = 80 + 45 = 125. Expected result: exactly 125, an integer and exact in binary floating point. Teeth: every price that IS in the list produces a total far from both 125 and 10 - 35*8+45 = 325, 18*8+45 = 189, 52*8+45 = 461, 27*8+45 = 261 - so a lookup that lands on a real row is nowhere near, and an approximate-match lookup with the fourth argument dropped walks to the LAST key, because "P-99" outranks "P-14" at the second character after the hyphen, returning 27 and therefore 261 rather than 125. Because the fallback is a RATE rather than a zero, the two commonest amputations are caught as well: dropping the quantity gives 10 + 45 = 55, and dropping the shipping gives 10 * 8 = 80, neither of which is 125. (This is why the fallback is not 0. With a zero fallback the whole product collapses, and a formula that never multiplied by the quantity at all would land on the same total as the correct one - the task would then be unable to tell whether the quantity had been used.) An unguarded lookup leaves #N/A and is not a number at all, so under-guarding is caught here too, unlike in errguard-ifna-keeps-divide-error-visible where the required answer is itself an error.

tasks.intent: Cell D2 must total the kWh column B2:B7. One of the six meters did not report this month and its cell holds the not-available error #N/A; that one reading must simply be left out of the total. D2 must end up holding a NUMBER - the total of the readings that are available - and must not itself become an error just because one cell in the range is one.

distractor.why: The reflex total, which is exactly what the intent rules out. SUM does not skip an error in its range, it inherits it: one #N/A anywhere in B2:B7 makes the whole sum #N/A, so D2 shows an error rather than the number 95. The failure is semantic and total rather than partial - it is not that the answer is 12 kWh light, it is that there is no answer at all, and one silent meter has taken the entire monthly report with it. That contagion is the thing this task exists to test, and the fix is a total that is told to ignore errors (AGGREGATE with option 6) or one that neutralises them cell by cell before adding, such as SUM(IFERROR(B2:B7,0)), which lands on the same 95. The guard-too-late spelling, =IFERROR(SUM(B2:B7),0), was measured on this fixture as well and returns 0: the error is already inside the sum by the time the guard sees it, so the whole month reads as zero consumption.

tasks.handCheck: By hand. B3 was entered as the literal #N/A, which the product's typed-entry ladder stores as a real error value rather than as the three-character text (core/engine/src/typed_entry.rs:181-186 is the rung for exactly this, and its own comment names the failure mode it was added to stop: storing it as text made ISNA FALSE, IFERROR pass it through, ISTEXT TRUE and COUNTA count a string). The grader seeds fixtures through that same ladder (core/calcula-format/src/ai/formula_verify.rs:219 calls engine::typed_entry::parse_cell_input), and on this fixture ISNA(B3) was measured TRUE and ISTEXT(B3) FALSE, so the premise is checked rather than assumed. So B3 is the error #N/A; the other five cells are plain numbers: B2 = 12, B4 = 18, B5 = 25, B6 = 31, B7 = 9. AGGREGATE's first argument 9 selects SUM and its second argument 6 is the option 'ignore error values', so the #N/A in B3 is excluded from the set being added and the remaining five are summed: 12 + 18 = 30, 30 + 25 = 55, 55 + 31 = 86, 86 + 9 = 95. Expected result: exactly 95, an integer and exact in binary floating point. Teeth: the excluded reading is deliberately NOT zero-like in the eye - a reader cannot check the total by ignoring a blank - and the grand total including a phantom value for M-02 would differ from 95 by whatever that phantom is, so no plausible mis-handling of the missing cell lands on 95. Cross-checked independently through a second correct spelling, SUM(IFERROR(B2:B7,0)), which turns the #N/A into 0 and adds 12 + 0 + 18 + 25 + 31 + 9 = 95: two different mechanisms, same number. One engine divergence found while checking this fixture and recorded here rather than left as a surprise: =SUBTOTAL(9,B2:B7) also returns 95 in Calcula, whereas Excel propagates the error through SUBTOTAL and would answer #N/A, so that spelling is scored correct by this task for a reason Excel would not agree with. The task itself does not rest on it - the reference is AGGREGATE and the distractor is SUM - but the divergence (and the matching one in COUNT, which returns #N/A here where Excel ignores errors and returns 5) belongs in the bug ledger, not in this corpus.

tasks.intent: Cell E4 must show how much of the Research budget is still unspent: the budget in B4 minus the actual in C4. Research has not reported an actual yet, so C4 is completely empty - and for as long as that is true E4 must show nothing at all, an empty text string, rather than a number. It must specifically NOT report the full budget as unspent and must not show a zero either. Once an actual is entered, E4 shows the difference as a number.

distractor.why: Guarding against an error when the thing to guard against is a BLANK. An empty cell is not an error: in arithmetic it is coerced to 0, so B4-C4 is 4000 - 0 = 4000, a perfectly ordinary number. IFERROR never fires, the empty second argument is never reached, and E4 reports 4000 - that Research has spent nothing and has its entire budget intact. That is a statement about the world the sheet has no evidence for; the true state is that nobody has reported yet. The distractor is wrong by 4000 against a required empty string, and it is wrong in the dangerous direction, because a missing report and a report of zero spending look identical in the total at the bottom of the column. Only a test that asks about emptiness - ISBLANK, or a comparison of C4 with "" - can tell the two apart. The IFNA-shaped version, =IFNA(B4-C4,""), was measured on this fixture too and likewise returns 4000, so the confusion is caught rather than one spelling of it.

tasks.handCheck: By hand. The Research row is row 4: B4 holds 4000 and there is no C4 cell at all in the fixture, so C4 is genuinely empty. ISBLANK(C4) asks whether that cell is empty and was measured TRUE. The IF takes its SECOND argument, the empty string literal "", so E4 holds a zero-length piece of text and displays as nothing. Expected result: text, the empty string. Teeth: every other row in the fixture HAS an actual, and each produces a distinct non-zero difference - Sales 4000 - 3600 = 400, Support 2500 - 2500 = 0, Logistics 3100 - 2900 = 200 - so the correct formula pointed at any other row returns a number, and row 4 is the only one where the blank branch is taken. Note that the Support row deliberately gives a genuine 0: a reader can see that 'shows nothing' and 'shows zero' are different outcomes that both occur in this fixture, which is what makes the distinction the intent draws a real one rather than a stylistic preference. One lenience, recorded rather than hidden: =IF(C4=0,"",B4-C4) also yields the empty string here, because an empty cell coerces to 0 in the comparison and the test is TRUE. So this cell does NOT measure the zero-versus-blank confusion - it measures the blank-versus-error one, and zero-versus-blank is what errguard-countblank-missing-timesheets is for. Note also that =IF(C4="","",B4-C4) is a legitimately correct alternative here and was measured at the empty string; that the same "" comparison is the DISTRACTOR in errguard-isblank-vs-empty-string-audit is deliberate - it is right when the cell is truly empty and wrong when the cell holds a formula returning "", so no blanket rule about it survives the family.

tasks.intent: The Enquiries sheet lists the customer behind every order in A2:A10, and several customers placed more than one order. In D2, use one formula that returns ONLY the customers that appear exactly once in A2:A10 -- a customer with two or more orders must not appear at all, not even once -- keeping them in the order they first appear in the column. Let the result spill down.

distractor.why: This is the DE-DUPLICATE reading of the request instead of the appears-exactly-once reading. With the third argument absent, fn_unique defaults exactly_once to false (evaluator.rs:10047-10054) and unique_vectors takes its first-occurrence branch (evaluator.rs:10141-10148), so every distinct customer survives -- including the repeat buyers the intent excludes. It spills Nordic Ltd, Bergsson, Castellan, Duvall, Ellison: 5 rows instead of 2, anchored on "Nordic Ltd", the customer with the MOST orders, rather than "Duvall". The two readings are as far apart as this fixture allows: the de-duplicate answer's anchor is a three-order customer, the correct answer's anchor is a one-order customer.

tasks.handCheck: Count each customer in A2:A10 by hand: Nordic Ltd appears at rows 2, 4 and 8 = 3 times; Bergsson at rows 3 and 6 = 2; Castellan at rows 5 and 10 = 2; Duvall at row 7 = 1; Ellison at row 9 = 1. Nine rows, five distinct names, 3+2+2+1+1 = 9, so the census is complete. UNIQUE(A2:A10, by_col=FALSE, exactly_once=TRUE) reads its third argument as a boolean (evaluator.rs:10047-10053) and hands exactly_once=true to unique_vectors, which first tallies the key of every row and then keeps a row only when its count is exactly 1 (evaluator.rs:10126-10139). Only Duvall (count 1) and Ellison (count 1) pass; Nordic Ltd, Bergsson and Castellan are all dropped ENTIRELY, which is the difference from ordinary de-duplication. Surviving rows keep their original order of appearance because the retain loop walks the input vector in order, so Duvall (row 7) precedes Ellison (row 9). The source is a single column, so cols==1 and UNIQUE returns a FLAT array (evaluator.rs:10071-10072). Spill = 2 rows x 1 column, anchor D2 = "Duvall". Pure text selection, no arithmetic. Column B is present only so the fixture reads like a real order list; no formula touches it.

tasks.intent: In E2, use one formula to list the member names from A2:A9 for every row that satisfies EITHER of two conditions -- the Tier in column B is Gold, OR the Points in column C are above 500 -- so a member who meets just one of the two still qualifies. Keep the rows in their original sheet order and let the result spill down.

distractor.why: The two conditions are right and so are the ranges; the JOIN is wrong. Multiplying the two Boolean arrays is AND -- a row survives only when BOTH tests are 1 -- so it keeps only Eklund (Gold and 910) and Grigg (Gold and 770), 2 rows instead of 5, anchored on "Eklund". It silently drops the three members the OR reading exists to catch: Brandt (Gold but only 80 points), Cheng (640 points but Bronze) and Haas (505 points but Silver). The fixture is built so the * and + answers cannot coincide: the first row either reading keeps differs (Brandt at row 3 for +, Eklund at row 6 for *), so the anchor separates them even before the row counts do.

tasks.handCheck: Comparison operators lift over ranges, so (B2:B9="Gold") and (C2:C9>500) are each an 8x1 Boolean array, and + adds them elementwise with Boolean->1.0/0.0. Row by row, writing (tier test)+(points test): Alvarez 0+0=0 EXCLUDED; Brandt 1+0=1 KEPT (Gold, 80 points); Cheng 0+1=1 KEPT (Bronze, 640 > 500); Dahl 0+0=0 EXCLUDED (300 is not above 500); Eklund 1+1=2 KEPT; Fournier 0+0=0 EXCLUDED; Grigg 1+1=2 KEPT; Haas 0+1=1 KEPT (505 > 500). Five rows survive. The two rows that score 2 matter: fn_filter's truthiness test is `EvalResult::Number(n) => *n != 0.0` (evaluator.rs:9742-9745), so 2 is just as truthy as 1 and a row meeting both conditions is kept ONCE, not twice -- summing Booleans is a safe spelling of OR here. get_range_dimensions measures the include argument from the VALUE, giving inc_rows=8, inc_cols=1 against rows=8, so FILTER takes the filter_by_row branch (evaluator.rs:9727-9731). FILTER preserves sheet order and, because the filtered array A2:A9 has cols==1, returns a flat array (evaluator.rs:9765-9767): {"Brandt";"Cheng";"Eklund";"Grigg";"Haas"}. Spill = 5 rows x 1 column, anchor E2 = "Brandt". Alvarez (Silver, 120), Dahl (Silver, 300) and Fournier (Bronze, 200) are the three rows no reading keeps -- each fails BOTH tests, which is why neither the OR nor the AND reading admits them; Haas at 505 pins the strictness of > 500 only mildly, which is deliberate -- this task tests the OR, not the boundary.

tasks.intent: In E2, use one formula that returns the whole three-column block A2:C7 -- Machine, Line and Units together, all three columns -- with the rows reordered from the highest Units in column C down to the lowest. Do not include the header row and do not change which columns appear or their order. Let the result spill down and across.

distractor.why: The sort_index points at the wrong column. 1 means "sort by the FIRST column of the array", which here is Machine, not Units -- and because the array starts at column A, the index is positional within the array, not the sheet column letter. Sorting the machine NAMES descending is a text sort on the uppercased key (evaluator.rs:9940), giving ZETA, GAMMA, EPSILON, DELTA, BETA, ALPHA, so the anchor E2 reads "Zeta" instead of "Beta" and the Units column comes out in the meaningless order 820, 275, 150, 640, 980, 410. In EXCEL a model reaches the same wrong answer by omitting the sort_index -- =SORT(A2:C7,,-1) defaults it to 1 -- but that spelling must not be used as the distractor here, because Calcula rejects the empty slot and answers #VALUE! (BUG-0114, verified against the engine on this very fixture); that is an engine defect rather than a semantic mistake, and it would go toothless the day the bug is fixed. The distractor is therefore written out in full. A second wrong form fails on the anchor too: =SORT(A2:C7,3,1) sorts by the right column in the wrong direction and anchors on "Epsilon", the 150-unit machine.

tasks.handCheck: The array is A2:C7 = 6 rows x 3 columns, so sort_index 3 selects the third column OF THE ARRAY, which is C (Units); the bound check sort_index <= cols passes with 3 <= 3 (evaluator.rs:9853-9856). The six Units values are Alpha 410, Beta 980, Gamma 275, Delta 640, Epsilon 150, Zeta 820. All six are Numbers, so compare_eval_results puts every one in sort class 0 and compares them numerically (evaluator.rs:9939), and sort_order -1 reverses that comparison (evaluator.rs:9870-9871). Descending: 980 Beta, 820 Zeta, 640 Delta, 410 Alpha, 275 Gamma, 150 Epsilon. All six keys are distinct integers, so the ordering is total and no tie rule can be reached. SORT moves WHOLE ROWS -- row_vecs are built as complete 3-value rows before the sort and reassembled afterwards (evaluator.rs:9858-9878) -- so Beta keeps its own Line 2 and 980 and the block stays internally consistent. cols is 3, not 1, so the result is an Array of row-Arrays (evaluator.rs:9876-9877): a 6 row x 3 column spill whose top-left cell is the Machine name of the highest-output row. Anchor E2 = "Beta". Header row 1 is excluded by the range; including it would drag the TEXT "Units" into the key column, where text outranks every number (class 1 beats class 0) and under a reversed sort would surface at the top, making the anchor "Machine".

tasks.intent: The four quarterly revenue figures sit SIDE BY SIDE in one row, B2:E2, under the quarter headers in B1:E1. In B5, use one formula that lists those same four numbers as a single VERTICAL column running down from B5, ordered from smallest to largest. Do not return the quarter headers, only the four revenue numbers.

distractor.why: It sorts the source where it lies instead of standing it upright first, and on a horizontal range that is a NO-OP. SORT's default orientation is by_col=FALSE, meaning "reorder the ROWS, using column sort_index as the key" (evaluator.rs:9835-9842). B2:E2 is 1 row x 4 columns, so there is exactly one row to reorder and the sort changes nothing: the result is the original left-to-right run 540, 310, 880, 725, still horizontal, anchored on 540 -- Q1, which is neither the smallest nor in any sorted position. Nothing errors and nothing is flagged, which is what makes this mistake expensive: sort_index defaults to 1 and 1 is inside bounds (1 <= 4 columns), so the formula looks like it worked. The fixture deliberately puts a MIDDLE value in Q1 rather than the smallest, so that leaving the row untransposed is visible at the anchor; had Q1 held 310, the no-op would have produced the right anchor by accident. The same anchor also catches transposing without sorting -- =TRANSPOSE(B2:E2) is a correct vertical column in the WRONG order and anchors on 540 too -- and sorting the wrong way, since =SORT(TRANSPOSE(B2:E2),1,-1) anchors on 880.

tasks.handCheck: The four revenues in sheet order are Q1 540, Q2 310, Q3 880, Q4 725. TRANSPOSE(B2:E2) reads the range as rows=1, cols=4 and re-emits it index by index as cols x rows (evaluator.rs:8758-8773), producing a 4 row x 1 column array {540;310;880;725} -- the same four numbers, now standing upright, which is precisely what SORT needs, because SORT's default orientation reorders ROWS and a one-row input has nothing to reorder. SORT then measures that value as 4 rows x 1 column; sort_index defaults to 1 (evaluator.rs:9819-9826) and names the only column, passing the bound check 1 <= 1, and sort_order defaults to 1 = ascending (evaluator.rs:9827-9834), which is what the intent asks for, so no optional argument has to be written at all. All four keys are Numbers, sort class 0, compared numerically (evaluator.rs:9939). Ascending: 310, 540, 725, 880. All four are distinct integers, so the order is total and no tie rule can be reached; each is a small integer exactly representable in binary floating point, so no rounding decision exists. cols==1, so SORT returns a flat array (evaluator.rs:9874-9875): a 4 row x 1 column spill down B5:B8. tasks.intent: The Signups sheet holds TWO separate name lists that do not sit next to each other: the morning session in A2:A6 and the evening session in C2:C5. Nobody is signed up twice, so nothing has to be removed. Let the result spill down.

distractor.why: It treats two separate lists as ONE rectangle. A2:C6 is the bounding box of both blocks, so it drags in the empty column B and the empty C6, and SORT's default orientation reorders ROWS keyed on column 1 -- the morning names -- carrying each row's unrelated evening name along for the ride. The result is a 5 row x 3 column block rather than a single column of nine names: Chandra/blank/Ahlberg, Ibarra/blank/Grimaldi, Pelletier/blank/Tanaka, Ramirez/blank/Novak, Winslow/blank/blank. Four of the nine people are reachable only in a third column, each paired with a stranger, and the four evening names are in no alphabetical order at all. The anchor E2 reads "Chandra", the alphabetically first MORNING name, instead of "Ahlberg". The same anchor catches the lazier miss =SORT(A2:A6), which forgets the evening list outright and also anchors on Chandra.

tasks.handCheck: The nine names are the five in A2:A6 -- Ramirez, Chandra, Pelletier, Ibarra, Winslow -- and the four in C2:C5 -- Novak, Ahlberg, Tanaka, Grimaldi. VSTACK(A2:A6,C2:C5) puts the second block UNDER the first, producing one 9 row x 1 column array in the order Ramirez, Chandra, Pelletier, Ibarra, Winslow, Novak, Ahlberg, Tanaka, Grimaldi; 5 + 4 = 9, so nobody is lost or doubled. SORT then measures that VALUE as 9 rows x 1 column, so the default sort_index 1 names the only column and passes the bound check 1 <= 1, and the default sort_order 1 is ascending -- both defaults are exactly what the intent asks for, so no optional argument has to be written and the BUG-0114 empty-slot spelling never arises. All nine keys are text, sort class 1, compared on the uppercased string. Their first letters A, C, G, I, N, P, R, T, W are all distinct, so the comparison never looks past character one and the order is total with no tie rule reachable: AHLBERG, CHANDRA, GRIMALDI, IBARRA, NOVAK, PELLETIER, RAMIREZ, TANAKA, WINSLOW. The source has cols==1, so SORT returns a flat array: a 9 row x 1 column spill down E2:E10, anchor E2 = "Ahlberg". The fixture deliberately puts the alphabetically first name overall in the SECOND list -- Ahlberg is an evening signup -- so any formula that reads only the morning block anchors on Chandra and is caught. Because the stacking happens BEFORE the sort, the stacking order does not matter: =SORT(VSTACK(C2:C5,A2:A6)) is equally correct and also anchors on Ahlberg (measured), and a redundant UNIQUE around the stack is harmless because all nine names are distinct (measured). One limit a reader should know rather than discover: the anchor cannot catch the mirror-image mistake. =SORT(C2:C5), reading only the EVENING list, anchors on "Ahlberg" as well and would grade as correct. No anchor can catch both omissions at once, because the anchor value lives in exactly one of the two blocks; the fixture is oriented to punish the likelier error, which is reading the first list and stopping.

tasks.intent: The Fleet sheet holds four columns in A1:D8: Asset number, Vehicle, Depot and Mileage. Keep the vehicles in their original sheet order and let the result spill down and across.

The spill is 3 x 4 rather than 3 x 2, its first column is the Asset number, and the anchor G2 therefore reads the NUMBER 4102 instead of the text "Van 12" -- a different value and a different type. tasks.intent: The sheet lists five gauges that were checked in March (column B) and again in April (column C). In E2, report how spread out the APRIL readings in C2:C6 are — their standard deviation. Treat those five gauges as a SAMPLE drawn from the plant's much larger stock of gauges rather than as the whole population, so the summed squared deviations are divided by one less than the count.

distractor.why: STDEVP is the POPULATION standard deviation: it divides the summed squared deviations by n rather than by n-1, which is the wrong denominator for five gauges treated as a sample of a larger stock. The summed squared deviations are 100, so STDEVP returns SQRT(100/5) = SQRT(20) = 4.47213595499958 where the sample answer is SQRT(100/4) = 5 — 10.6% too small, and low in the direction that matters, because a population divisor always understates the spread of a sample. Two further traps this fixture catches: =VAR(C2:C6) stops at the variance and returns 25, the square of the answer rather than the answer; and =STDEV(B2:B6) reads the March column instead, returning SQRT(90/4) = 4.743416490252569 — a mistake the fixture makes invisible to a sanity check on the mean, because March and April both average exactly 20.

tasks.handCheck: April readings C2:C6 = 13, 19, 20, 21, 27. Sum = 13+19 = 32; +20 = 52; +21 = 73; +27 = 100. n = 5, so the mean is 100/5 = 20 exactly. Deviations from 20: -7, -1, 0, 1, 7. Squares: 49, 1, 0, 1, 49. Summed squared deviations = 49+1 = 50; +0 = 50; +1 = 51; +49 = 100. Sample variance = 100/(5-1) = 25 exactly; sample standard deviation = SQRT(25) = 5 exactly. Every intermediate is a small integer, so nothing rounds in IEEE-754 doubles and the engine returns 5 with no residue. The population figures for contrast: variance 100/5 = 20, standard deviation SQRT(20) = 4.47213595499958 (recomputed independently in double precision, not copied from the engine). March B2:B6 = 14, 17, 20, 23, 26 also sums to 100 and so also has mean 20, but its deviations are -6, -3, 0, 3, 6, giving summed squares 36+9+0+9+36 = 90, sample variance 22.5 and standard deviation SQRT(22.5) = 4.743416490252569.

tasks.intent: B2:B11 records how many parcels each of ten delivery runs carried. In D2, report the parcel count that comes up MOST OFTEN across the ten runs — the value with the highest frequency. Exactly one count occurs more often than any other, so there is no tie to break.

The ten counts sort to 4, 6, 6, 6, 6, 9, 9, 9, 11, 13; with an even count the median averages the 5th and 6th, (6+9)/2 = 7.5, which is not even one of the recorded counts, let alone the most frequent one. The fixture is built so the three plausible 'typical value' functions are all distinct: MODE = 6, MEDIAN = 7.5, AVERAGE = 79/10 = 7.9. It also puts the mode strictly between the extremes — MIN is 4 and MAX is 13 — so neither of those coincides with the answer either, and it gives 9 a runner-up frequency of three so that a formula picking the most common value has to count rather than eyeball.

Tally: 6 appears in B2, B4, B8 and B11 — four times; 9 appears in B3, B7 and B10 — three times; 13, 4 and 11 appear once each. 4 + 3 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 10, so every row is accounted for. The highest frequency is four, held by 6 alone, so MODE = 6 and there is no tie for the engine's first-encountered rule to decide. Checks on the distractor and the near misses: sorted the list is 4, 6, 6, 6, 6, 9, 9, 9, 11, 13; n = 10 is even so MEDIAN = (5th + 6th)/2 = (6 + 9)/2 = 7.5. Sum = 6+9 = 15; +6 = 21; +13 = 34; +4 = 38; +9 = 47; +6 = 53; +11 = 64; +9 = 73; +6 = 79, so AVERAGE = 7.9. MIN = 4, MAX = 13.

tasks.intent: B2:B10 holds the number of minutes it took to send a first reply to each of nine support tickets. In D2, report the 90th percentile of those nine times. Use the inclusive definition — the one in which the 0th percentile is the smallest value in the list and the 100th percentile is the largest — and interpolate between the two ranked values that the 90% point falls between rather than snapping to the nearest recorded ticket. Give the percentile as a plain number of minutes.

distractor.why: This is the 'count 90% of the rows' reading: 90% of nine tickets is 8.1, so the reasoning goes, take the 8th-slowest — the 2nd-largest — and call that the 90th percentile. LARGE(...,2) returns 25, the recorded time of ticket T-08, where the interpolated 90th percentile is 32. A percentile is a position on the scale of VALUES, not a row picked out of a ranked list, and on this fixture the gap between the top two tickets (25 and 60) is wide enough that the distinction is worth 7 minutes. Two further traps the fixture catches: =PERCENTILE(B2:B10,90) passes the percentile as 90 rather than as the fraction 0.9 and returns #NUM!; and =MEDIAN(B2:B10) answers the 50th percentile, 12.

tasks.handCheck: The nine times are already ascending: 4, 6, 7, 9, 12, 15, 18, 25, 60. Under the inclusive definition the sorted values sit at percentiles 0, 1/8, 2/8, ... 8/8, so the 90% point is at the zero-based rank p*(n-1) = 0.9*(9-1) = 7.2. Rank 7 (zero-based) is the 8th smallest value, 25; rank 8 is the 9th, 60. The fractional part 0.2 interpolates linearly between them: 25 + 0.2*(60-25) = 25 + 0.2*35 = 25 + 7 = 32 minutes. Sanity checks on the neighbours: the 7.2 lands above rank 7, so the answer must exceed 25, and below rank 8, so it must fall short of 60 — 32 satisfies both. Floating point: 0.9 has no exact binary representation, so 0.9*8 evaluates to 7.200000000000000177..., the fraction comes out as 0.2000000000000001776 rather than 0.2, and the engine returns 32.00000000000001. The grader's default tolerance is relative, DEFAULT_TOLERANCE = 1e-9 scaled by the magnitude (core/calcula-format/src/ai/formula_verify.rs:582), which allows about 3.2e-8 here against an actual gap of 1.1e-14, so the expectation is written as the exact 32. For contrast, the EXCLUSIVE definition would place the 90% point at rank p*(n+1) = 9, i.e. the largest value 60, which is why the intent pins the inclusive one.

tasks.intent: B2:B7 holds six months of advertising spend and C2:C7 the sales booked in the same six months, both in thousands. In E2, report the correlation coefficient between spend and sales — the unitless number between -1 and 1 that says how tightly the two move together — rounded to 4 decimal places.

distractor.why: RSQ is the coefficient of DETERMINATION, r squared — the share of the variation in sales the fitted line accounts for — not the correlation coefficient r itself. It returns 0.8537 where r is 0.9239. Squaring always pulls a correlation toward zero, so r squared reads as a weaker relationship than the data shows, and it also throws away the sign, which is the whole point of a correlation coefficient. A further trap the fixture catches: =SLOPE(C2:C7,B2:B7) returns exactly 2, the extra thousand of sales per thousand of spend — a rate with units, which changes if the columns are rescaled, whereas r does not. Note that argument ORDER is NOT a trap here: unlike SLOPE and INTERCEPT, CORREL is symmetric, and the engine returns 0.9239364353597956 for both =CORREL(B2:B7,C2:C7) and =CORREL(C2:C7,B2:B7).

tasks.handCheck: Spend x = 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60: sum = 210, n = 6, mean = 35 exactly. Sales y = 150, 140, 190, 190, 240, 230: sum = 150+140 = 290; +190 = 480; +190 = 670; +240 = 910; +230 = 1140, mean = 1140/6 = 190 exactly. Deviations dx = -25, -15, -5, 5, 15, 25 and dy = -40, -50, 0, 0, 50, 40. Cross products dx*dy = 1000, 750, 0, 0, 750, 1000, so Sxy = 3500. Squares dx^2 = 625, 225, 25, 25, 225, 625, so Sxx = 1750. Squares dy^2 = 1600, 2500, 0, 0, 2500, 1600, so Syy = 8200. r = Sxy / SQRT(Sxx*Syy) = 3500 / SQRT(1750*8200) = 3500 / SQRT(14350000) = 3500 / 3788.139384975162 = 0.9239364353597956 (recomputed independently in double precision). ROUND to 4 places: (0.9239364353597956 * 10000).round()/10000 = 9239.364353597956 rounds to 9239, /10000 = 0.9239. Not a halfway case, so the round-half-away-from-zero convention does not bite. The distractor's value falls out of the same numbers: r squared = Sxy^2/(Sxx*Syy) = 12250000/14350000 = 35/41 = 0.8536585365853658, which rounds to 0.8537. Both means being whole numbers is what keeps every deviation an exact integer, so the only inexact step in the whole derivation is the single square root.

tasks.intent: B2:B7 holds the machine hours run in each of six months and C2:C7 the electricity bill for the same months. The bill is a fixed standing charge plus a variable amount per machine hour. In E2, work out the FIXED standing charge: fit a least-squares straight line through all six months, with Bill as the value being predicted and Machine hours as the predictor, and report what that line says the bill would be at zero machine hours. The six months do not sit exactly on the line, so all six must go into the fit — not the cheapest month on its own, and not any single pair of months.

distractor.why: INTERCEPT takes known_y first and known_x second, the same order as SLOPE. Writing the x range first regresses machine hours ON the bill instead, which answers 'how many machine hours would a zero-kronor bill imply' — a question with no business meaning — and returns 70 - (56000/452800)*2060 = -184.77031802120143. A negative standing charge is the giveaway, but nothing in the sheet flags it. Two further traps the fixture catches, both of them ways of answering with a single point instead of a fit: =MIN(C2:C7) treats the cheapest month as the fixed cost and returns 1680, forgetting that January still ran 20 hours of variable load; and the high-low method =C2-(C7-C2)/(B7-B2)*B2 uses only the first and last months, 1680 - (760/100)*20, and returns 1528. Both are close enough to 1500 to pass a glance and neither is the least-squares answer.

tasks.handCheck: The intercept of a least-squares fit is mean_y - slope*mean_x. Hours x = 20, 40, 60, 80, 100, 120: sum = 420, n = 6, mean_x = 70 exactly. Bills y = 1680, 1780, 2000, 2120, 2340, 2440: sum = 1680+1780 = 3460; +2000 = 5460; +2120 = 7580; +2340 = 9920; +2440 = 12360, mean_y = 12360/6 = 2060 exactly. Deviations dx = -50, -30, -10, 10, 30, 50 and dy = -380, -280, -60, 60, 280, 380. Cross products dx*dy = 19000, 8400, 600, 600, 8400, 19000, so Sxy = 19000+8400 = 27400; +600 = 28000; +600 = 28600; +8400 = 37000; +19000 = 56000. Squares dx^2 = 2500, 900, 100, 100, 900, 2500, so Sxx = 7000. slope = 56000/7000 = 8 exactly — 8 per machine hour. intercept = 2060 - 8*70 = 2060 - 560 = 1500 exactly. Both means are whole numbers and every intermediate is an integer, so nothing rounds in IEEE-754 doubles. The fitted line is Bill = 1500 + 8*Hours, and NOT ONE of the six months sits exactly on it: the predictions are 1660, 1820, 1980, 2140, 2300, 2460 against actuals 1680, 1780, 2000, 2120, 2340, 2440, so the residuals are +20, -40, +20, -20, +40, -20. Those residuals sum to zero and their cross product with the hour deviations is (-50)(20)+(-30)(-40)+(-10)(20)+(10)(-20)+(30)(40)+(50)(-20) = -1000+1200-200-200+1200-1000 = 0, which is exactly the pair of conditions that makes 8 and 1500 the least-squares fit rather than some other line. Because every month is off the line, no single pair of months reproduces the fit either. The swapped-argument figure: Syy = 380^2+280^2+60^2+60^2+280^2+380^2 = 144400+78400+3600+3600+78400+144400 = 452800, so the reversed slope is 56000/452800 = 0.1236749116607774 and the reversed intercept is 70 - 0.1236749116607774*2060 = 70 - 254.77031802120143 = -184.77031802120143 (recomputed independently in double precision).

tasks.intent: B1:B5 describes a savings plan: B1 is the amount already sitting in the account today, B2 the deposit made at the END of every month, B3 the annual interest rate, B4 the number of years and B5 the number of deposits per year. In D2, report the balance at the end of the term, rounded to 2 decimals. Use the monthly rate (annual rate divided by deposits per year) and the total number of deposits (years times deposits per year). Follow the spreadsheet sign convention: money going IN is entered as a negative amount — that applies to the monthly deposit AND to the balance already in the account — so that the closing balance comes out POSITIVE. The opening balance earns interest for the whole term, so it is part of the calculation, not something to add on afterwards at face value.

distractor.why: It drops the present value argument, so the 10000 already in the account is never carried forward: the answer is the future value of the deposits alone, 58377.67 instead of 73047.88. The shortfall is 14670.21, which is not the 10000 that was forgotten but 10000 grown at 0.4% a month for 96 months — which is why adding 10000 back by hand afterwards does not repair it either and leaves the answer 4670.21 short. Two further traps the fixture catches. Sign: =ROUND(FV(B3/B5,B4*B5,B2,B1),2) enters the deposits and the opening balance as positive and returns -73047.88, the right magnitude with the wrong sign, which is the commonest way this function is misread. Rate per period: =ROUND(FV(B3,B4*B5,-B2,-B1),2) feeds the ANNUAL 4.8% into a calculation that still counts 96 monthly periods and returns 1828948.56, twenty-five times the true balance.

tasks.handCheck: rate = B3/B5 = 0.048/12 = 0.004 exactly (the engine confirms 0.004 with no residue, because 0.048/12 is the nearest double to 0.004). nper = B4*B5 = 8*12 = 96. pmt = -500, pv = -10000, type omitted, so payments fall at the END of each month. FV(rate, nper, pmt, pv) = -(pv*(1+rate)^nper + pmt*((1+rate)^nper - 1)/rate). Growth factor (1.004)^96 = 1.467021334317669 (recomputed independently with Math.pow in double precision, not read off the engine). The opening balance contributes -(-10000)*1.467021334317669 = 14670.21334317669. The annuity factor is ((1.467021334317669 - 1)/0.004) = 0.467021334317669/0.004 = 116.75533357941725, so the deposits contribute -(-500)*116.75533357941725 = 58377.66678970862. Total = 14670.21334317669 + 58377.66678970862 = 73047.88013288532. fn_round computes (73047.88013288532 * 100).round()/100 = (7304788.013288532).round()/100 = 7304788/100 = 73047.88. Not a halfway case. Cross-check on the magnitude: 96 deposits of 500 is 48000 of principal plus the 10000 opening balance, 58000 in all, so 73047.88 represents 15047.88 of interest over eight years — about 26% on money that averages roughly half the term in the account at 4.8%, which is the right order. The distractor's 58377.67 is the annuity leg alone, and 73047.88 - 58377.67 = 14670.21 is exactly the compounded opening balance.

tasks.intent: A1:B8 is a project's cash flow by year: B2 is the Year 0 outlay, B3:B7 are the net cash flows at the end of Years 1 to 5, and row 8 is a Total, which is a summary and not a cash flow. In D2, report the project's internal rate of return — the annual discount rate at which the whole series, Year 0 included, has a net present value of zero. Unlike NPV, the Year 0 outlay belongs INSIDE the series here, because the function reads its first value as the flow at time zero and discounts nothing. Give the rate as a decimal fraction rounded to 4 decimal places, so that 0.0825 would mean 8.25%. Leave the Total row out.

distractor.why: Extending the range to B8 swallows the Total row, and IRR cannot tell a summary from a cash flow: it reads the total 29000 as a SIXTH year of inflow. That phantom flow is the project's whole undiscounted net profit (-60000+15000+18000+22000+25000+9000 = 29000) arriving a second time, at the end of Year 6. The series then appears to return 0.2194 instead of 0.1492 — 22% a year for a project that actually yields 15%, a 7-point overstatement that still looks like a believable project return, which is why this survives review. A further trap the fixture catches runs the other way: =IRR(B3:B7) applies the NPV rule — 'the Year 0 outlay sits outside the function' — to IRR, where it is wrong. IRR needs the outlay inside, and without it the series is all positive, no discount rate can bring it to zero, and the engine returns #NUM! rather than a number.
